title: Breaking: David Jones staff issued with redundancy notices
text:
More than 1,600 David Jones staff have been issued with redundancy notices today.

The notices, received by 1,689 employees, inform them their employment will officially terminate on December 30.

The union, the Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees' Association (SDA), says it will be working overtime to assist members to find alternative employment.

The iconic retailer went into voluntary administration earlier this month.

title: Cricketers' association slams 'disgraceful' treatment of Sandpapergate players
text:
The CEO of the Australian Cricketers' Association, Paul Marsh, has labelled the media treatment of Australian Test players as "absolutely disgraceful".

Marsh has criticised the media coverage of players linked to the 2018 Sandpapergate scandal which has seen media teams taking videos and photos outside players' houses, most notably of Australia's Test captain, Pat Cummins.

"We've got media camped outside and hounding players' families in their private homes and with their personal activities and it's disgraceful in my view," Marsh told ABC Sport.

"This has been an issue where people's integrity's being questioned, left, right and centre."

The union leader has called for the media companies to consider their actions

"There's a human toll to this that I think is being disregarded in a lot of quarters," he said.

"The scrutiny, the accusations, the fact their families are being hounded here, like, this is really difficult.

"I'm really concerned about the players' well-being at the moment as a collective.

"The reality of this is, this is hurting I think everyone that's involved."

Steve Smith says he did not want to speak to the press on his return to the New South Wales set-up ahead of Sunday's Shield game. (Supplied: Channel 10)

Questions around who knew details of the 2018 Cape Town sandpaper plot have blown up in the past two weeks since the publication of Usman Khawaja's memoir, and a newspaper article by the player at the centre of the scandal, Cameron Bancroft.

Bancroft said that the entire 2018 team knew about the sandpaper plot.

Those allegations directly contradict other Australian players who played in the 2018 tour including Cummins, who held an extensive media conference denying any knowledge of the sandpaper plot.

Marsh is calling for space and perspective.

"Understandably people want to understand that the black and white of what might have happened here but I'm just not convinced we're going to get to that," he said.

"What I do think we need to do is find a way to get the players and others that were involved together and talk about this and actually try to find a way through.

"I do think that they might need everyone here to give a bit."

Pat Cummins spoke in front of a press conference for 68 minutes, but has also been door-stopped outside his home. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

He said mistakes were made by all parties in 2018 that are adding to the current febrile environment.

"I think there was a lot of pressure put on the team at the time from Cricket Australia, and I think they need to take some responsibility," Marsh said.

"I think time again, maybe the whole playing group should have taken a collective responsibility for this, whether they knew or they didn't know.

"I think that also needs to be an understanding that one person's recollection of what happened here, might be different to somebody else's — [that] doesn't mean that anyone's not telling the truth."

Cricket Australia (CA) this week announced the formation of a forum to allow players to discuss their recollection of events in 2018 behind closed doors.

But the proposal has been criticised because it won't take the form of an inquiry to find a set of agreed facts and because the CA board will decide what it will and won't release after the forum is completed.

CA hasn't released the terms of reference for the forum, nor has it named a person to oversee it.

Marsh said while he was supporting the attempt to find a way to move forward, he said he was still waiting on the details of the forum.

Steve Smith has not made any comments since the release of Usman Khawaja's book, Sabr. (Supplied: Channel 10)

"I'd probably rather understand exactly what they're proposing before I get into assessing it," he said.

He said the Australian players want what's best for Australian cricket.

"Let's work out how we can get there because if we don't do that, I feel like we're going to stay in the place that we're at the moment, which is hurting everyone," he added.

He said while he accepted the public want to know who knew what regarding the sandpaper plot, that may be impossible.

"I think we all would love to have a, you know, an accepted set of facts, but the reality of this is we don't," he said.

"I've had lots of conversations with players the last two weeks, and you know, players with no reason to tell me any differently than what is the truth.

"Players are saying, 'I don't remember the meeting that's been referred to here' or the next person saying, 'I think we had that meeting', and this is what we're dealing with at the moment.

"I would just ask consider the human element of what these guys are going through at the moment."

title: Fifth Melbourne Cup revealed as stolen after 'staggering' heists
text:
Six Melbourne and Caulfield cups are missing, it can be revealed, as the Victoria Racing Club (VRC) comes under fire by racing insiders over cup carnival security measures.

The ABC can reveal that in addition to four Melbourne Cups and one Caulfield Cup stolen in the recent heists during the peak of this year's racing carnival, the 1973 Melbourne Cup, which was stolen from Flemington several years ago, has never been found.

The late jockey Frank Reys became the first Indigenous jockey to win the historic race with Australian thoroughbred gelding Gala Supreme.

Years after Reys' death from cancer in 1984, his family donated the cup to the VRC.

Frank Reys was the first and remains the only Aboriginal man to win the Melbourne Cup. (Supplied: Isabella Tolhurst)

The ABC understands it was stolen from its display near the exclusive Committee Room at Flemington Racecourse, but the exact date of the theft remains unclear.

The theft was reported to police but the cup was never recovered.

Darren Hutchins, whose grandfather trained winning runner Gala Supreme, told the ABC it was "pretty disappointing" that five additional cups had been stolen years after the one belonging to his grandfather's winner had also been swiped.

"To have one disappear is horrific … but to have four more disappear, where's the accountability around this?" he said.

"I just think it's horrendous that this could be allowed to happen.

"It seems like it was pretty easy to access them and get away with it.

" I just find it staggering that the level of security was as lax as it must've been. "

It comes after police charged two men, Sama Mirzaagha and Chrysovalandis Tassakos, over the recent Flemington and Caulfield heists.

The 1948 Caulfield Cup won by Red Fury was stolen from Caulfield Racecourse between November 4 and November 11, along with bottles of wine and other "low-value" items.

The ABC understands the Caulfield Cup has been melted down; with fears the stolen Melbourne Cups have also suffered the same fate.

A replica Melbourne Cup was allegedly stolen from Flemington on November 12.

Four days later, alleged thieves dressed as tradies swiped legendary Makybe Diva's three consecutive Melbourne Cups worth $3 million.

Call to replace stolen Makybe Diva cups

Mr Hutchins called on the VRC to disclose the level of security they had employed to guard the stolen cups, in addition to CCTV and alarms that were triggered during the alleged robberies at Flemington.

"Transparency's key … I don't think they have anything to hide," he said.

"I think they'd be better off coming out and saying what's happened," he said.

"Just be up-front and tell people exactly what's gone on."

Darren Hutchins has questioned the security at Flemington Racecourse following the recent heists. (ABC News: Scott Jewell)

Mr Hutchins also called on the VRC to remake Makybe Diva's cups if the originals were permanently lost or melted down, because owner Tony Santic had loaned the trophies to them during this year's cup carnival.

"If they don't find these within a timely manner, then replace them … with proper models, not duped up dummies," he said.

"A replacement's the least they could do."

Charged with burglary, theft, and dealing with property suspected of being the proceeds of crime over the Flemington robberies, Mr Mirzaagha was remanded following a brief magistrates court hearing yesterday.

Mr Tassakos was charged over the alleged thefts at both venues and was bailed.

The pair will return to court in February.

Mr Hutchins said he hoped the recent spate of alleged thefts would reignite the search for the 1973 Melbourne Cup.

"I hope it hasn't been melted because they're just irreplaceable items," he said.

The VRC declined to comment.

title: 'Completely flattened': Farmers count their losses after wild storm
text:
Shed doors were blown off and crops wiped out during a "rare" storm supercell that flattened major electricity transmission towers on South Australia's Eyre Peninsula.

Locals are surveying the damage caused by severe winds which tore across the region, cutting power to about 24,000 properties at 3pm on Thursday.

Wharminda resident Sarah Prime stood outside her home watching the wild weather sweep over her paddocks, a scene she described like something out of a Ridley Scott movie.

"All of a sudden, everything in the backyard was just lifting up and whizzing around, and I actually went and got our dog — I thought she was going to blow away," she said.

With November prime harvest time for many across the state, the timing was not welcomed.

Crops were destroyed during the storm. (Supplied: Caleb Prime )

"There are some areas that are completely flattened, and you know, bits of the crop are hanging in trees or over the power lines and things like that," Ms Prime said.

"There are parts that will be affected but not damaged as badly, and then there'll be other parts that aren't touched at all."

Sarah's brother-in-law Jarrod Prime was working in his shed when the wind ripped its 600-kilogram door off its hinges.

"I just started running for my life up at the other end of the shed," he said.

Jarrod Prime says he has never seen anything like Thursday's conditions in his 20 years of farming. (ABC News: Stephen Opie)

"It was a pretty harrowing experience, the worst I have ever felt.

"I'm very distraught with the damage, but luckily everyone is safe."

ElectraNet said the significant winds brought down two major transmission towers and damaged a third — infrastructure that was only upgraded three years ago.

Transmission towers and powerlines were taken out by strong winds. (Supplied: Caleb Prime)

Grain Producers SA chief executive Brad Perry said farmers were assessing damage and it was too early to know if the storm had impacted harvest figures this year.

"We certainly feel for those growers," he told SA Country Hour.

"It's looking like a record crop and suddenly having it on the ground is devastating," he said.

Storm swept across Arno Bay yesterday. (Supplied: Nathan Sprinks)

Local businesses lose thousands

Arno Bay Jetty Cafe owner Kath Tayler said her losses were already over $10,000 and could reach $20,000 depending on the weather in the coming days.

The cafe's freezers are currently unable to connect to her small generator.

"I'm too scared to open the big freezer room because I'm not sure what we're going to find," she said.

Many Arno Bay businesses are in the same boat. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jenae Madden)

"Depending on what happens with the big freezer room … if it's [stock] just defrosted, we can still use it, we just can't obviously refreeze it.

" We also had a milk order delivery that came this morning … so that milk is still sitting out in the shop, just getting hot, so we'll lose all that as well plus what's already in the fridges. "

Power progressively being restored

While a large portion of the region had their lights back on, just over 1000 properties remained without power as at 4:45pm on Friday, according to SA Power Networks's outage map.

At Friday's press conference, SA Premier Peter Malinauskas said a bypass line was being installed to connect the West Coast and Upper Eyre Peninsula "later today".

Temporary measures to bring supply back are also underway, including crane installations to "re-erect" the transmission line and temporary tower installations in the coming days.

Peter Malinauskas says power could be restored to Eyre Peninsula as soon as today. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

A 20-megawatt generator located in Port Lincoln has been powering the township and lower Eyre Peninsula since Thursday night.

All residents in the area have been urged to turn off their solar panels to ensure the generator does not exceed its level of demand.

Mr Malinauskas said while it was great news the generator was working as it should, there were other risks ahead.

"We're not out of the woods yet, there is still storm events coming our way, extreme fire conditions over the course of the weekend," he said.

"The generator itself is temperamental in nature. It is in a very old piece of equipment and we should be alive to the prospect that that may fail, and that's why we continue to monitor it."

Towers were up to standard

ElectraNet executive network manager Alex Trento said the transmission towers that fell were designed to withstand up to around 170km/h wind speed.

"The design of these towers are also tested to destruction, that is to the actual design standard that they're meant to abide by," he said.

Mr Trento said he did not know what the wind speed was when the towers toppled but the probability of it occurring was "very rare".

Alex Trento says the towers were designed appropriately. (ABC News: Lincoln Rothall)

When asked if there could be a reason other than strong winds that knock down the towers, Mr Trento said structural fault in the towers was "a possibility" and ElectraNet was investigating.

"At this point in time, seeing the localisation of the event, we do think that the towers have been designed and constructed effectively," he said.

ElectraNet expected an estimate of the cost of repairs to be available "in the next three to six months".

Mr Malinauskas confirmed the state government would also be reviewing what had occurred over the past 24 hours.

"There will be an appropriate examination of ElectraNet's infrastructure and why it's failed under these circumstances," he said.

title: How often do sheets, pillows and mattresses need cleaning?
text:
Getting into a freshly made bed is one of life's small joys, but when things get busy, regularly cleaning your bedding can get overlooked.

While changing your sheets is pretty manageable, experts say cleaning your pillows, mattresses and quilts regularly is also important, particularly if there are people in your home with allergies.

But how often you need to clean them depends on a variety of factors. Here's what the experts say.

Sweat, skin cells and creepy-crawlies

As we sleep, our bodies shed sweat, oils, fats and skin cells, all of which end up in our beds, says associate professor Rietie Venter, who works on the traditional lands of Kaurna people at Adelaide University's School of Pharmacy and Biomedical Sciences.

"And all those things can contain microbes … especially our skin cells," Dr Venter says.

Cleaning your bedding is a way to remove the "microbial load", as well as dealing with smells and creating a comfortable place to sleep, she says.

Cleaning pet beds in washing machines Ever wondered about the wisdom of running your pet's bedding through your washing machine? We asked the experts about how hygienic it is.

For many people, the microbes in their beds won't do much harm.

"[But] even though those microbes might not be the worst … you still don't want to cuddle each night in a whole lot of microbes, especially if you're prone to allergies or you're a bit immunocompromised," Dr Venter says.

Cleaning your bedding also helps control dust mites, which feed on dead skin, love moisture, and can cause severe allergies in some people, says Stephen Doggett, director of medical entomology with NSW Health Pathology at Westmead Hospital in Sydney/Dharug country.

How often should you clean your sheets?

Unless you're immunocompromised or allergic to dust mites, Dr Venter says how often you clean your sheets and pillow cases really comes down to personal preference.

Washing your sheets and bedding removes oils, skin cells and microbes, Rietie Venter says. (Unsplash)

She says for a person who showers before bed, wears pyjamas and isn't a heavy sweater, "probably once every two weeks would be good enough".

"Otherwise, once every week," she says.

And if you sleep naked, you may want to wash more frequently, Dr Venter says.

What about your pillow?

Matthew Steen, director of testing for consumer group Choice, says pillows should be cleaned about every six months, as a benchmark, and how you do it depends on what it's made of.

In general, he says:

Memory foam should be spot cleaned.

Latex should be handwashed.

Polyester, cotton or microfibre needs a warm machine wash.

Down or feathers should be hand washed or dry cleaned.

"They'll often give you recommendations on the tag," which should be followed, he adds.

Cleaning methods for pillows differ depending on what they are made of. (Unsplash)

When it comes to replacing your pillow, Mr Steen says there's no hard and fast rule, and if it's been regularly cleaned, it's more about whether the pillow is still comfortable.

Choice research recently found that only polyester pillows provided replacement time frames.

"And we cannot find any evidence to back up those dates," Mr Steen adds.

For those allergic to dust mites, "put the pillow into a hot air dryer for 20 minutes and that'll kill most of the mites", Dr Doggett says.

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

How to clean a mattress

Mr Steen recommends regularly sprinkling the surface with bicarb soda and leaving it to absorb smells, then running a vacuum cleaner over the surface and putting it out in the sun.

For light to moderate stains on a mattress or mattress topper, he suggests rubbing or blotting using gentle detergent, upholstery or enzyme cleaner, or diluted vinegar with a soft cloth and "a very light touch".

Mattresses should be flipped and rotated regularly to avoid wear and sagging in one spot. (Unsplash)

He also recommends rotating your mattress frequently to prevent wear in one spot and flipping it (if it doesn't have a built-in topper that prevents flipping).

Cleaning your mattress twice a year is a good benchmark, Mr Steen says, but there's no hard rule on when to replace it.

"Are you getting sore? That's my sign, personally," he says.

"If you're finding that it's not as comfortable, then it's pretty much time, or [if] you're physically seeing sags."

Extending the life of your mattress We asked the experts how we can extend the life of a mattress, including dealing with accidents and stains, and when it might be time to upgrade.

These considerations also apply to mattress toppers, he says.

When it comes to cleaning a mattress topper, Mr Steen says many are machine washable, but they can be quite heavy, "so you might want to see if your machine is actually capable of doing it".

"Definitely follow the instructions on that," he says.

Dr Doggett says mattress and pillow cleaning is particularly important for people who have an allergy to dust mites, as it keeps mite numbers down and removes the dead skin they feed on.

There are also encasing mattress and pillow covers on the market that make them impermeable to dust mites.

Cleaning doonas or quilts

Doonas and quilts made from microfibres and natural materials such as cotton are machine washable, Mr Steen says, adding most will fit in a regular washing machine if the air has been squished out.

But there are some quilts and doonas that can't be machine washed.

"Definitely look at the [washing] instructions … If they've said not to wash it, you're stuck with however they're deciding to tell you how to do it," Mr Steen says.

He recommends cleaning doonas and quilts twice a year and replacing them when they stop keeping you warm or become uncomfortable.

Quilt covers can be washed more frequently, in the same way as sheets and pillowcases.

title: Former SA Health worker 'inappropriately accessed' 503 patient records
text:
SA Health has revealed that a former staff member inappropriately accessed 503 patient records since September 2024.

A formal investigation was launched after SA Health was notified of a privacy breach in late June.

It says the Yorke and Northern Local Health Network (YNLHN) staff member was immediately put on leave when the investigation began and no longer works for SA Health.

In a statement, SA Health said the incident had been reported to the relevant authorities, and the staff member will have "a note on their permanent record".

Patients notified

SA Health says all affected patients have been notified in writing by the YNLHN.

"SA Health has policies and processes in place to ensure staff only access information that is necessary and appropriate for their role," the statement read.

"This includes requiring staff to verify they are authorised to access the information when they log into the electronic medical record system."

SA Health says it's considering additional measures to prevent further breaches, including strengthening audits for potential inappropriate access to patient information. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

The statement noted additional measures were being explored to prevent further breaches, and that any staff member accessing information without a legitimate work-related reason may be subject to disciplinary processes, including possible employment termination.

YNLHN chief executive Zoe Bishop said the Network sincerely apologises for any harm and distress caused.

"Any unauthorised access of information is taken very seriously, and after a careful and comprehensive investigation process, the staff member is no longer employed by SA Health," Dr Bishop wrote in a statement.

"We acted as soon as we were made aware of these potential breaches.

"I want to reassure the community that this behaviour falls well below the standards we expect, and people should continue to have trust in our health services and our hardworking staff."

Robyn Lindsay is the Department for Health and Wellbeing's chief executive. (Supplied)

Department for Health and Wellbeing chief executive Robyn Lindsay said the "vast majority" of SA Health staff access patient information appropriately.

"Where we find that a patient's information has been inappropriately accessed, we have a responsibility to inform the patients of the breach and take appropriate action during and after the investigation," she wrote.

"While breaches such as this are rare, we must continue to remain vigilant to ensure we maintain the highest possible standards of integrity when it relates to patient information."

In a separate incident in July, SA Health apologised to the family of Tony Modra amid revelations staff may have inappropriately accessed his patient records.

Multiple staff members were being investigated at the time for alleged privacy breaches.

In December 2024, 18 SA Health staff members resigned or were sanctioned for unauthorised access to the records of Charlie Stevens, the late son of Grant Stevens.

SA Health reports quarterly on staff members who have been reprimanded or terminated from their employment for inappropriately accessing patient records.

title: AFLW physicality helps resilient Tayla Harris 'feel alive'
text:
Tayla Harris has always been a player for the big moments.

The Melbourne forward is renowned for high-flying marks and picture-perfect kicks.

But with Melbourne down by seven points in the fourth quarter of its qualifying final against Geelong, it was Harris's grit that delivered.

Harris, knowing how ex-Melbourne coach Mick Stinear talks about the inside and outside layers of a contest, realised Cats star Nina Morrison would win the ball in the latter.

She made her move, flattening Morrison with a perfectly timed, legal and brutal bump.

It set the tone as Tom Wilson's Melbourne completed a turnaround from 28 points down to beat Geelong and reach Saturday's preliminary final against Carlton at Princes Park.

"That's how I play," Harris said.

Tayla Harris's physicality isn't always reflected in the stats. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Martin Keep)

"I would like to think that people know that I only ever play with fair intent.

"And our game requires some pretty impactful moments.

"And I'll cop it back, no problem — and I do often. A few Geelong players got me good.

"Hell yeah, this is how I feel alive."

Harris, 29, knows her impact goes beyond the stat sheet.

"What I do with my physicality and presence I know has an impact on our team in a positive way, so I'll continue to do whatever's required in that moment," she said.

"If it's putting your body on the line, if it's spoiling or if it's running hard, whatever it might require, all of us would agree that, particularly in finals, those little moments matter."

Two years ago, bumping and clunking overhead marks appeared a pipe dream.

Tayla Harris struggled with injuries to her shoulders 12 months ago. (Getty Images: Kelly Defina)

The ruck-forward had surgery on her loose shoulders, one after the other, but never doubted she would return.

"I'm pretty determined when it comes to overcoming adversity or being told that I can't," Harris said.

"I'm pretty bullish on proving to myself that I can."

Having dealt with two trades, plus a failed trade to Hawthorn and a rise to fame and highly publicised social media abuse, there is not much Harris can not handle.

"My career hasn't been one that's been straightforward and all roses, which I'm really thankful for because it builds resilience," Harris said.

"And the adversity that I have faced has made me a better player, but more importantly, person.

"When it was hitting the fan, it's all happening. And then you feel like the world's collapsing in and then next minute it's all good again. But that's life."

Harris practises breathwork and maintains her boxing fitness, a throwback to a childhood that juggled football with waterskiing and skateboarding.

"I'd spend hours on the street trying to do a kickflip, and I'd fail 100 times, and then I would maybe get one and think that I was Tony Hawk," she said.

"I'm so glad that I grew up that way and with my parents not letting me believe that failure was a bad thing — it was just part of it.

"The only way that you're ever going to get anywhere is to fail.

"One thing I know for sure is I will continue to get it wrong and continue to make mistakes and continue to fail, so to speak, but that's the only way I'll ever keep growing or get better."

Inaugural AFLW star Harris would love to play for several more years.

But first, the 2022 premiership winner wants another flag.

"We believe we can go all the way. But we are absolutely set on this next game that we have," Harris said.

"We recently watched a Kobe Bryant press conference and they'd gone up 2-0 in the playoffs and the journalist had said 'why aren't you smiling?'

"And he's got a straight face and goes, 'Job's not done.'

"So that's our philosophy at the moment and we're certainly not looking ahead. But we certainly believe."

AAP

title: Brisbane 2032 whitewater venue makes political waves as costs kept secret
text:
The cost of the canoe slalom venue for the Brisbane 2032 Olympic and Paralympic Games venue has been kept secret, as the whitewater facility becomes a flashpoint in the local mayoral race.

The state government has refused to reveal individual costs for most Games venues, but Jarrod Bleijie assured the Redland Whitewater Centre was within the $7.1 billion funding envelope.

"We want to save taxpayer money, so we want competitive tension in the market, and we found that with competitive tension in the market, it drives down the cost."

Deputy Premier Jarrod Bleijie says the cost of the centre will come within the $7.1b olympic funding budget. (ABC News)

The centre, east of Brisbane, will host rafting and canoe slalom, with designers behind the Tokyo 2020 and Rio 2016 whitewater facilities selected to oversee the project.

Marketed as Redland "South Bank", the facility will form part of a recreational precinct after the Games and serve as a training hub for the State Emergency Service.

Queensland Fire Department Commissioner Steve Smith said emergency responders currently had to travel to Far North Queensland or Tasmania to prepare.

"Realistic training is critical to safe and effective operations for us, no matter where we are functioning and operating," he said.

"And if you look just at last season, there were over 160 people rescued from swiftwater environments for various events right across Queensland."

Political stoush making waves

Outside the venue announcement, protesters gathered to oppose the development, including Redland City mayoral candidate Don Brown.

The former Labor state MP is running for the local post after Jos Mitchell stepped down in October, alleging a coordinated smear campaign against her.

Don Brown has pledged to pull "every single lever" to stop the facility if elected as Redland City mayor. (ABC News: Laura Lavelle)

He has made opposing the whitewater centre a core tenet of his election campaign, claiming it will push up rates and harm the local fauna.

"Every single lever, I'll be pulling everything, lobbying everyone, to make sure that this project does not go ahead.

"It's a luxury our ratepayers cannot afford.

"We believe in the legacy of the site, protecting 650 koala trees here and enhancing it into the future."

But Mr Bleijie rubbished the claim.

"Don Brown's just running a misinformation campaign," he said.

The venue has attracted opposition in the community. (ABC News)

Early works are expected to get underway at the site next year, with the goal for the site to host the inaugural 2030 World Paddle Games.

Three-time Olympic gold medallist in canoe slalom, Jess Fox, said the site would attract athletes from across the globe while boosting local interest.

"We can see kids starting to get on that development pathway.

Jess Fox says the facility will attract athletes from around the world. (Paddle Australia)

"We can have our national team, elite athletes, and interstate athletes coming to train here, to live here, to base themselves here, and international athletes who want to come and make the most of Queensland's beautiful weather and hospitality as well."

It comes as the government this week announced Brisbane's Victoria Park stadium was ahead of schedule, 100 days into earthworks.

title: Media locked out of Steve Smith training session at SCG
text:
Steve Smith has returned to training in a covert session with New South Wales as the hierarchy closes ranks around Australia's star batsman.

Smith arrived at the Sydney Cricket Ground today through a back entrance, and media were locked out of watching the ex-Test captain bat in the nets.

The 37-year-old has maintained his silence amid a fresh furore surrounding the sandpaper scandal.

After returning from New York earlier this week, Smith is expected to play for the Blues in their Sheffield Shield game against Queensland at the SCG starting on Sunday.

Smith has not played any cricket since suffering a neck injury in the second Test on last month's tour of South Africa.

Current Test captain Pat Cummins and his national cohorts Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon also could feature in the NSW side in the final round of Shield games before Australia name a squad for the first Test against New Zealand starting December 9.

Those four bowlers did not attend Blues training yesterday.

Smith has not spoken publicly since the release of Usman Khawaja's autobiography, which has triggered an unheralded split in Australian cricket.

Khawaja wrote that all players were aware of Australia's ball tampering in the infamous Test match against South Africa in 2018.

That version was rejected as nonsense by Cummins, but has been supported by David Warner, Cameron Bancroft and Chadd Sayers.

Cummins bluntly denied any knowledge of Australia using sandpaper on the ball in Cape Town.

But Bancroft, in a written account issued on Wednesday night, said all players knew the plan.

Smith, Test skipper at the time, was banned by Cricket Australia for 12 months and stripped of the captaincy.

Warner was also suspended for a year and removed from the vice-captaincy, while Bancroft, who was caught by television cameras in Cape Town with sandpaper, was banned for nine months.

AAP

title: General Pants owner warned of trouble long before collapse
text:
The owner of General Pants Co had been warned multiple times about the retailer's ability to keep operating long before the company collapsed into administration.

Documents seen by the ABC show Alquemie Group, which acquired General Pants Co in 2022, was told by auditors BDO its ongoing reliance on cash injections from shareholders, combined with challenging retail conditions, cast doubt on its ability to continue operating.

General Pants, which started as a jeans retailer in 1972, is the last remaining retailer of the group which once had six brands to its name, and was handed to administrators Alvarez & Marsal late on Wednesday evening.

Alquemie Group reported losses after tax shot up from $2 million in 2023 to $29.6 million in 2024 and $27.2 million in 2025.

General Pants was the last brand owned by Alquemie Group. (ABC NEWS: Michael Barnett)

During that time there was a management change, with the former chief executive of the now collapsed Mosaic Brands, Scott Evans, joining the group in May 2024 "with a clear mandate to restructure the business and return it to profitability", according to its financial report.

Following Mr Evans's appointment, the group sold loss-making companies SurfStitch and Ginger & Smart and shut the doors of National Geographic, which had cost it $4.4 million the year prior.

Alquemie also underwrote the value of the General Pants brand by $13.2 million, leaving its worth at $38.2 million, a far cry from the $60 million it paid to acquire the company.

General Pants Co in voluntary administration There are now 500 jobs in question as the administrators plan to continue trading through the busy Black Friday sales period.

It received a $14 million cash injection from private equity firms and key shareholders in 2024 and a second one of $8 million in 2025.

Even with the injection, the company continued to breach conditions with its main bank lender CBA, managing to carry the loans forward to avoid defaulting.

But during that process, its loans ballooned from $4.6 million in 2023 to $43.8 million in 2025.

Lego stores could not stem the bleeding

Alquemie sold its Lego Store business earlier this year. (AAP: Dean Lewins)

The group touted the excellent performance of its licensed Lego Stores yet sold the business for a reported $65 million to Kennedy Consolidated in May this year.

Company staff numbers were also slashed from 1,246 to 929.

The troubles did not stop there.

In 2024 logistics firm Mainfreight issued the company a winding-up order, saying it was owed $125,000, and supplier UCC did the same in 2025, saying it was owed almost $70,000.

Financial auditors raised concerns multiple times about Alquemie's ability to continue operating.

"Ongoing challenging conditions within the retail industry, compounded by the broader economic impacts of the cost of living crisis, have contributed to the Group producing a loss before tax of $31,955,000 for the financial year, resulting in a continued breach of covenants related to the Group's loan facility with CBA," BDO audit director Josh Bresolin wrote in the financial report.

It went on to say that outside factors affecting the business "were exacerbated by internal operational issues".

This included decisions within General Pants that led to subsequent operating losses "which, under new leadership, have subsequently been rectified".

It further pointed out that its debts, economic climate and customer sentiment indicated that "a material uncertainty exists that may cast significant doubt on the Group's ability to continue as a going concern".

An Alquemie Group spokesperson said the retail trading environment and the growing dominance of offshore online-only retailers had seen General Pants progressively reduce its physical store footprint.

"To address this, Alquemie Group actively focused on a range of options for General Pants including a sale process or significant capital injection to help it better compete against large scale competitors," they said.

"None were ultimately viable."

They said a voluntary administration process would explore restructuring scenarios which could allow General Pants the opportunity to be restructured into smaller-scale, more focused and, ultimately, viable business.

Retail sector struggles

QUT retail expert Gary Mortimer said retailers in the mid-price, casual fashion category, such as General Pants, were particularly struggling with external macro environmental changes.

"Consumers in general who would normally shop across these types of brands are now more concerned with putting food on the table, putting fuel in their car [and] paying their rental mortgage than they are with buying a new pair of jeans," Dr Mortimer said.

General Pants lists 158 different brands on its website. Of them, 14 are inhouse brands under different labels — something known as a phantom brand strategy.

Gary Mortimer says the mid-price fashion sector is struggling. (Supplied: Gary Mortimer)

While that can work in some sectors such as groceries, Dr Mortimer said it was challenging, particularly in youth fashion.

"Young people are very, very brand centric," he said.

"They want a brand that is well known, it has brand equity, it has brand value.

"While their styling may be on trend, if the brand doesn't resonate or is not easily recognised by their peer group, that then creates a subsequent challenge."

Ultra-fast fashion puts stores under pressure

CreditorWatch chief economist Ivan Colhoun said changes to the retail fashion sector, such as the rise of ultra-fast-fashion online stores, meant companies such as General Pants and David Jones might not have been in good health for some time.

"There's a number of other pressures that have changed in a structural sense, like working from home means that people were spending less time in CBDs," he said.

Black Friday has changed how people shop. (ABC News: Anna Chisholm)

" And then Black Friday is something that is changing when consumers spend their money and at what prices. "

He echoed Dr Mortimer's sentiment that rising interest rates meant discretionary spending was lower, and added that businesses with large amounts of debt would also have issues.

He said bricks and mortar retailers had also been hit by the rising freight costs — something exacerbated by the war in the Middle East.

Voluntary administration can be a good thing

Retail restructuring expert James Stewart said he was not surprised General Pants Co had gone into administration.

"The reality is … this market of voluntary administrations is possibly a sensible thing to do for a lot of organisations who just don't have a sustainable proposition at the moment," he said.

"If there is a restructuring, that could allow them to come out the other side of it in a better shape."

He said while parts of the retail sector were struggling, there were numerous companies bucking the trend, including beauty retailer Mecca, value-based retailers such as Kmart, and supermarkets.

"There's always retailers in any market that will do well and there's always ones that will struggle," he said.

"So there's no particular blanket rule that you can apply."

title: Farmers celebrate downpour in western NSW
text:
Pastoralists in the west of the state are celebrating a huge downpour of rain overnight, hailing it a "godsend" ahead of the dry summer forecast.

Garry Mooring, from Rose Isle station on the Darling-Baaka River north of Louth, said he had recorded 204 millimetres since midday yesterday.

"This will see us through the summer now, this rain," he said.

Farmers work in floodwater at Myandetta Station. (Supplied)

Mr Mooring said he had only ever once seen the river level increase so rapidly.

"The river has come up possibly 2 metres. We've been here 57 years, and I can only ever recall once the river rising that quick from local water," he said.

" There should be a lot of people delighted. "

Fears for summer eased

Further downstream, Stuart Le Lievre runs sheep and cattle on a station near Tilpa, where his rain gauges recorded between 85 and 140 millimetres.

"It's bloody wonderful," he said.

"It's been patchy, we got that break back in May and have bugger all since then. The country has held on remarkably well."

A station near Bourke has recorded 173mm of rain overnight. (Supplied)

He said the concerns he had ahead of summer had been put to rest entirely.

"We won't have to worry about summer now, that was our main worry because the Bureau [of Meteorology] were forecasting this really bad El Niño that was going to hit us like hell."

Vegetation across the region had been dying off slowly in the last few months before the rain fell.

"It's been a godsend, to be honest with you.

"It's wonderful for us and those that were lucky enough to get under it," Mr Le Lievre said.

Rapid rise for Darling-Baaka River

At Rose Isle, Mr Mooring said the rainwater tanks were overflowing and the river looked primed for a swim.

"It might be silty, but it's good-quality clean water in there amongst that silt," he said.

Caught off guard by how quickly the rain fell, he said the only casualty was a kayak that was swept away.

"The river rose that quickly; there's a kayak that's escaped. It's heading somewhere down the river, hopefully someone might get an eye on it."

Happily trapped

Despite both being trapped by road closures, Mr Mooring and Mr Le Lievre were happy.

Water lies over the road near Tibooburra. (Supplied)

"I don't think I'd even want to get out, it'll be a week before I could get out of here. But we've got plenty of food," said Mr Le Lievre.

Mr Mooring said he would happily stay trapped if the rain continues.

" I don't mind how long we're isolated for if it keeps raining. "

Water lies across a road in Thomson's Creek, near Tibooburra. (Supplied: Richard Norris )

Most unsealed roads and many sealed roads in the Far West are closed, with the Barrier Highway between Cockburn and Wilcannia, the Silver City Highway between Broken Hill and Wentworth, the Menindee Road between Broken Hill and Menindee and Silverton Roads all open under caution.

Labor has sold the digital duty of care as a way to try to regulate the tech sector, making social media platforms, AI chatbots, search engines and apps responsible for protecting adults and children from harmful content. Australian investors have received a fraction of the Anthropic shares they applied for, but those who bought into the artificial intelligence company enjoyed a 17 per cent value jump in the first day of trading on Friday. Despite a bad day on the market overall, the Claude-maker’s record-breaking IPO pushed the combined wealth of its seven co-founders to $US166 billion ($249 billion) as shares of the AI lab jumped following its debut. Sydney motor mechanic Nadav didn’t get all the shares he wanted in Anthropic, but was still happy to invest. Dominic Lorrimer The stock, priced at $US83 a share, soared to $US111.50 in early trade, giving the company a market capitalisation of more than $US2 trillion ($3 trillion) in early trade before paring gains. It closed at $US97.17 in New York trading, giving the company a value of about $US1.8 trillion ($2.7 trillion) and valuing each founder’s fortune at about $US24 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. The $US107.3 billion public offering and concurrent private placement broke SpaceX’s record for the biggest-ever.

Advertisement

Sydney mechanic Nadav, who declined to provide his surname, said he had received 7 per cent of the shares he had applied for via the online brokerage Stake. “With it being so oversubscribed, the majority of people didn’t get the allocation they were expecting, so I was a bit disappointed,” the 31-year-old said. But overall, he said, it was “exciting to be a part of it”. Some people who attempted to buy shares via other companies reportedly missed out altogether because demand was so strong. It is common for firms listing on the stock market to offer fewer shares than investors would ultimately like to ensure a “pop” in value, which can help to build momentum. After the listing, Nadav said he bought more shares in the company to take his holding up to 10, split between a personal account and superannuation fund. He said he regularly used AI tools, including Anthropic’s Claude, to run his garage and communicate with customers. “It makes sense I want the company to do well,” Nadav said.

Advertisement

Advertisement

Keeping things equal Anthropic has an unusually even ownership structure among its founders, with each holding about the same 1.3 per cent fully diluted economic stake in the firm. Despite their relatively small economic stakes, the founders retain outsized control over the company through Founder LLC, an entity that owns a single Class F share carrying 50.1 per cent of voting power. All seven have pledged to dedicate 80 per cent of their personal company equity to philanthropic causes, but that is not legally binding. A big step for Silicon Valley

Advertisement

Founded in January 2021 by former OpenAI employees, Anthropic was valued at $US461 million in its Series A funding round that year, according to PitchBook. Since then, its valuation has climbed more than 320,000 per cent, based on the fully diluted valuation implied by the offering price. Australian broking services and banks have made access to popular US public listings a point of distinction. On Friday, Stake’s website read “Anthropic has arrived” in bold text. Ashton Kutcher, pictured with wife Mila Kunis, is a big winner from the Anthropic float. Invision/AP Wealth managers Morgans, Bell Potter, LGT Wealth and Morgan Stanley all had access to the IPO in Australia, alongside online brokers Sharesies and CommSec. Jonathan Belz, chief executive of BFA Global Investors, said his firm had put about $30 million into Anthropic for its clients in multiple rounds before the public offering.

Advertisement

“Obviously, we haven’t exited yet, these things have escrow, so victory dances at first day IPO prices may be a little bit premature,” said Belz, whose firm invests on behalf of institutions and wealthy families. Related Article Updated

Wall Street ‘It doesn’t get better than this’: Anthropic mints thousands of instant millionaires He said that ordinary Australian investors clearly had not been prioritised either, noting he had heard of institutions that had asked for and received $US500 million in the IPO. “I wouldn’t say Australians were dudded,” Belz said, but added there was no strategic value for Anthropic in having these brokers get large allotments of shares for their clients. He said the firm and its bankers appeared to have prioritised investors who could make large commitments, big Anthropic customers, and its business partners. Retail investors have played an increasing role in the success of some technology stocks, including SpaceX, where charismatic founders have developed large fan bases.

The staggering sum of money that investors have poured into AI stocks this year has fuelled fears of a bubble. On Friday, the outgoing chairman of Australian AI data centre developer NextDC, Douglas Flynn, riffed on those worries. “Is it a bubble? Who knows? Nervousness surrounding AI continues to weigh down Wall Street. AP The All Ords, which comprises the most valuable 500 stocks on the ASX, fell 5.39 per cent over the week, wiping $169 billion of the index’s roughly $3.1 trillion market value in five sessions. All 11 local sectors ended the session lower, while only utilities have managed to keep out of the red since Monday.

Financial stocks ended sharply lower as the big four banks retreated. Commonwealth Bank fell 1 per cent, Westpac slumped 2.23 per cent, and National Australia Bank and ANZ Bank were down 1.31 per cent and 1.08 per cent respectively. Related Article Opinion

Health provider Monash IVF tumbled 23.84 per cent after it said its profit for the current financial year was expected to fall sharply below consensus estimates. The Australian dollar has continued its recent decline to buy US66.66¢, down from US66.89¢ on Thursday at 5pm, as risk sentiment continues to waver. Overnight, US indexes fell after an early morning recovery for beaten-down stocks tied to artificial intelligence quickly evaporated, with the S&P 500 dropping 2 per cent for a sixth straight loss. That is the index’s longest losing streak since 2024. It is down 8.2 per cent from its record set last month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 2.2 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite sank 2.3 per cent. The losses were widespread, and more than 90 per cent of the stocks that make up the S&P 500 fell. Anthropic surged at the open before paring its gains, but closed more than 17 per cent higher. AP Earlier in the morning, AI-related stocks seemed to be doing well enough. They had rallied after Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI chatbot, sold its stock at a price of $US83 each in its initial public offering. That’s more than the $US70 to $US78 it earlier thought it would get, and its price quickly surged above $US115 after it began trading on the Nasdaq shortly before noon. text:

Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears ASX Runners of the Week: Black Rock, Mayne Pharma & Metal Hawk Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Andrew Todd November 20, 2026 — 5:07pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. There’s only one word to describe markets this week… Carnage. As of mid-market Friday, the ASX is in the midst of its seventh straight losing session, a plunge of more than six per cent that has now wiped out every cent of its 2026 gains. This week’s Bulls N’ Bears ASX Runner of the Week is… Black Rock Mining. It is the worst run since the war kicked off in April, when oil shocks from Iran rocked the market. No doubt traderswould have closed the screens early on Friday and, at this rate, will be closing up shop completely by next week, as a sea of red continues to spread across almost every market and sector. Wall Street has fared no better, shedding around five per cent on the week, with the S&P 500 notching six straight losses and the Dow closing below 50,000 for the first time since June.

Advertisement

2027 can’t come soon enough. With no money to splash about on Christmas presents, the punters would probably be just as happy to hit the reset button on a bottomed-out economy and hope the new year brings a market rebound – and a few dollars back in their pockets to reinvest. Locally, they’re calling it a commod-apocalypse. As the AI trade continued to unravel and weak Chinese economic data added to the gloom this week, copper was the biggest casualty. Dr Copper, the economy’s bellwether, has fallen to US$5.57 a pound from US$6.65 just three weeks ago - 14 per cent - with Wednesday’s plunge its worst single-day fall since Trump tariff pandemonium. China’s October numbers also missed badly across the board, with retail sales growing just 0.4 per cent and investment shrinking 8.1 per cent. The AI sell-off and a flailing superpower in the east have sent jitters through a market increasingly hanging its hopes on data centre demand. Then gold joined the fray. Hawkish Fed minutes, a flight to cash and a surging US dollar sent the precious metal reaching for its emergency parachute. The shiny yellow metal said ‘Hold my beer’ and crashed to US$3525 an ounce by Friday. That’s a crippling seven per cent fall on the week, as Australian gold miners chalked up their own seventh straight session of hell. At this point, it might be better not to open the trading screen at all, to save shielding your eyes from the glowing crimson. AI offered no refuge in the end either. Nvidia posted revenue of US$115.8 billion (A$174 billion), more than double the year before and delivered a forecast above expectations. It still fell for a fifth straight session.

Advertisement

Even Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO couldn’t save the trade. Its blockbuster listing and public and private placements raised a whopping US$107.3 billion (A$161 billion), with Nvidia, Microsoft, Google and AMD all chipping in. The company briefly hit a US$2 trillion valuation on opening – more than SpaceX – before the broader sell-off dragged it back down too. Back home, Dr Jim Chalmers’ economy shed 44,000 jobs last month, pushing unemployment to 4.9 per cent - a five-year high - prompting headlines to declare what Runners had suggested seven weeks ago: Australia has one foot firmly in the recession bucket. After five rate hikes in seven meetings, government-induced inflation has done what everyone but the Labor government seemed to know it would: kill productivity and choke growth. Meanwhile, at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, the world’s leader Trump, Xi and even Putin held their first-ever three-way meeting, which unfortunately appeared to achieve little after Trump left early. Albo, who wasn’t in the room for that one, did get a moment of his own to tell Putin to end his war in Ukraine, after Australians broadly criticised the Prime Minister for posing for a group photo alongside the Russian president. On a week when almost the entire ASX was begging for the closing bell, only a handful of stocks managed to swim against the tide. A couple of small-cap miners, a pharmaceutical heavyweight and some spectacular gold grades were enough to earn a place among this week’s Runners. They managed to keep their heads above water for most of the week, before even the green shoots – bar a few in healthcare – were swallowed by the market sell-off on Friday. Black Rock Mining is pushing ahead with early works at its giant Mahenge graphite project in Tanzania after securing fresh funding.

Advertisement

BLACK ROCK MINING LTD (ASX: BKT) Up 125% (0.8c – 1.8c) Bulls N’ Bears Runner of the Week is Black Rock Mining, which surged after securing fresh funding in Tanzania to push ahead with early works at its giant Mahenge graphite project in the country’s south. The company says it has secured a US$5 million (A$7.5 million) early drawdown from Tanzanian bank CRDB, giving it the cash to mobilise contractors to site ahead of earthworks before the wet season arrives. It is a practical step towards construction, with Black Rock looking to have the groundwork in place for a rapid transition once the remaining financing is secured and a final investment decision is handed down, projected for early in the new year.

Advertisement

The company says plenty is happening on the funding front. Black Rock has reaffirmed a conditional US$40 million (A$60 million) equity commitment from South Korean industrial giant POSCO International and inked a non-binding deal with African Critical Minerals for a proposed US$70 million (A$105 million) cornerstone investment. Backed by South Africa’s Public Investment Corporation and Lionhead Capital Advisors, the proposed investment would help bankroll the first stage of Mahenge. Combined with existing debt and prepayment facilities, the various funding arrangements now account for US$258 million of the roughly US$298 million required for Module 1, leaving just US$40 million (A$60 million) to close the gap. Mahenge itself is no small operation, boasting a 213.1-million-tonne resource grading 7.8 per cent total graphitic carbon, including a 70.5-million-tonne ore reserve at 8.5 per cent. Its access to Tanzania’s hydro-dominated electricity grid is a key development advantage, with competitively priced power key to keeping operating costs in the lowest-cost quartile. The next pre-final investment decision phase is expected to include further front-end engineering design and tendering for the transmission line contracts, as PowerPoint plans turn to foundations on the ground. With contractors preparing to mobilise and most of the initial funding requirement now identified, Black Rock is edging closer to the big one: financial close and a construction decision.

Advertisement

MAYNE PHARMA GROUP LTD (ASX: MYX) Up 85% ($3.30 - $6.10) Snagging silver on the Runners podium and back dominating the headlines this week was Aussie pharmaceutical manufacturer Mayne Pharma Group, after agreeing to a $604 million cash takeover by the $10 billion-plus Hungarian pharmaceutical heavyweight Gedeon Richter. The takeover offered $6.40 a share, representing a whopping 99.4 per cent premium to its previous closing price and124 per cent above the 30-day volume-weighted average price for the languishing South Australian manufacturer. Richter has operations in roughly 50 countries and says Mayne’s established US commercial presence and product portfolio is the perfect platform to expand its women’s health business globally.

Advertisement

Mayne’s board has unanimously backed the deal, subject to the usual conditions and no superior proposal emerging. But there is plenty of fine print. The scheme is conditional on Mayne completing the sale of its international business to Evaris, while Richter has an exit provision if Mayne’s underlying EBITDA falls by more than $12 million in the current financial year. That is worth keeping an eye on, given Mayne generated $34.2 million in EBITDA last year. The deal also comes with a sizeable dose of déjà vu. In February last year, US-based Cosette Pharmaceuticals agreed to buy Mayne for $7.40 a share, valuing the company at about $672 million. That deal descended into a legal stoush after Cosette sought to walk away, alleging a material adverse change in Mayne’s earnings and sales performance. Mayne took the fight to the NSW Supreme Court; however, the deal was ultimately blocked by Federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers on national interest grounds, with concerns raised about local jobs, critical medical supply chains and Mayne’s long-standing Adelaide manufacturing facility. The Cosette saga ended in December, leaving shareholders back at square one. This time around, the proposed Richter transaction does not require FIRB approval, although the sale of Mayne’s international arm remains subject to its own approvals.

Advertisement

For shareholders who have endured the previous takeover drama, a cash offer at a hefty premium will no doubt be welcome. But with conditions still to be satisfied, the paperwork not quite finished, it’s doubtful long-term holders will be celebrating early. A drill rig on site at Metal Hawk’s Numbat prospect within its broader Leinster South project in WA. METAL HAWK LIMITED (ASX: MHK) Up 62% (13c – 21c) Rounding out this week’s Runners podium is WA gold explorer Metal Hawk, which has struck grades capable of making even the most battered gold market this week sit up and take notice.

Advertisement

The company says it delivered its richest gold results yet from the emerging Numbat shear discovery at the company’s Leinster South project, including a spectacular 11-metre hit grading 48.3 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 103m, featuring a blistering six-metre run at 81.2g/t. That sort of grade tends to cut through even the ugliest market sell-off and could even make the US$500-an-ounce gold prices of the 20th century look positively palatable. There is also serious thickness behind it, with other holes returning 4m at 28.5g/t and a broader 27m at 5.7g/t from the project’s south, at its Thylacine area. Metal Hawk says its latest 11-metre intersection sits 60m further down-plunge from its initial discovery holes, with hopes the structure could be strengthening and even emerging into a much bigger gold system with room to grow. What makes the results particularly interesting is where the gold is turning up. Earlier exploration had largely focused on the quartz veins at Numbat, where the richest mineralisation is usually found. However, the latest drilling has repeatedly returned gold from the surrounding sheared dolerite and gabbro, with significant intersections in every hole drilled beneath the earlier shear discovery. In other words, the quartz lode may only be part of the story. Metal Hawk is now investigating whether the surrounding sheared rocks host a much broader gold-bearing system, rather than being confined to a narrow run of high-grade quartz.

Advertisement

Leinster South sits in one of WA’s established gold districts, with major operators surrounding the junior explorer and plenty of regional mining infrastructure nearby. That is a handy postcode for any discovery, particularly if Metal Hawk can demonstrate that the Numbat mineralisation has the continuity and scale to attract a bigger audience. The company has already extended its diamond drilling campaign to follow up the latest results and test the broader system. Gold prices may be having a rough trot, but grades of 81.2g/t across handy widths tend to do their own talking, no matter how ugly the market gets. There are few, if any, who can manipulate a ruck quite like Harry Grant – his exploits in helping deliver another Rugby League World Cup triumph to Australia highlighting that, and adding weight to the Titans’ pursuit of the star hooker. But Gold Coast five-eighth Jayden Campbell has stressed that as much as Grant would add to a young and developing roster, assurances needed to be made that he – and any other prospective recruits – would be arriving at the Glitter Strip for the sole purpose of delivering glory to a region which has been deprived of it. “I’ve grown up on the Gold Coast, the Gold Coast has looked after me and my family, and I just want to give back to the Titans and bring success to the Titans,” Campbell said. Harry Grant is a man in demand, however the Titans have downplayed a pursuit publicly, with chief executive Steve Mitchell saying “There are probably 17 clubs who are going ‘is it worth having a chat to Harry?’” Getty Images “I want people at the Titans for the right reasons and to win as well, I’m not saying anyone doesn’t, but hopefully people come for the right reasons and see we’re on the up.”

Advertisement

The Titans have a history of making big money moves in recruitment to no avail – Jarryd Hayne, Shannon Boyd and David Fifita among those whose careers went downhill at the club. But Grant would be a different beast. Grant was instrumental in the Kangaroos’ 32-12 triumph of New Zealand at Suncorp Stadium’s World Cup final, orchestrating the way his side overcame their size disadvantage in the forward pack by exploiting tired markers and putting the likes of Cameron Munster and Jacob Preston into space behind the ruck. His deception laid on the first try of the night within 85 seconds when he faked to his left and fired a pass for Liam Martin to his right. The 28-year-old’s identification of weary defenders was on show earlier in the semi-final against Samoa when he set up Reece Walsh. Grant maintained he would delay contract talks until after the World Cup, having not taken a player option in his favour for 2028 with Melbourne. He is expected to command north of $1 million a season, and will have no shortage of options on the open market; with some reports suggesting he could seek a lifestyle change.

Advertisement

A feather in the Gold Coast’s cap could be his close relationship with minority owner Matthew Johns. Campbell appreciated the role Grant could play in educating a squad short on experience, and a spine consisting of himself, Zane Harrison (aged 20) and Keano Kini (22). The club – who have played just two finals games in the past 16 seasons – is also expected to lean on their junior talent in the forward pack; Arama Hau and Bodhi Sharpley set for more responsibility alongside Tino Fa’asuamaleaui, Moeaki Fotuaika and Beau Fermor.

Advertisement

But the son of club legend Preston Campbell – who shared similar sentiments with this masthead – believed the Titans had strong No.9 options in Oliver Pascoe and emerging teenager Jai Bilish, and a push for Grant’s signature needed to be fuelled by the dummy-half’s premiership desire; which Grant alluded in the build up to Sunday’s World Cup decider. “It’d be silly for any club to not look at Harry Grant – look at the type of player he is, and what he’s done in the game so far. But we’ve got a really good hooker in Ollie at our club now, he was one of our best players last year,” Campbell said. Jayden Campbell knows how valuable Harry Grant could be, but wants assurance a potential move would be to benefit the club more than a lifestyle change. “Having someone like Harry Grant at any club would be great, but what we’ve got now I’m really happy with, and I’m sure the coaching staff are happy with. We’ve got Ollie and Jai Bilish coming through, so no disrespect to any player or anything, but I’m really happy with what we’ve got, and we just want to work with what we’ve got now.” His father Preston added earlier: “If we can maintain that spine and the boys get to play alongside each other and get to understand each other a little bit more, we’re going to start seeing some more wins.”

Advertisement

Related Article Analysis

NRL 2026 The new face, the student and the veteran: The battle to succeed Reynolds Campbell has cast his eye on building on his fledgling halves combination with Harrison, as he revealed he spent the latter stages of 2026 playing through injury. Campbell said he would begin his preseason continuing his rehabilitation, but was aiming to be training in full after Christmas ahead of the Gold Coast’s maiden appearance in Las Vegas for round one. “I had to get my knee cleaned out at the end of the year, and then I was dealing with a turf toe injury at the back of the year, and it ended up being a few ligaments and a few cracked bones,” Campbell said. “I was playing with it for about eight weeks, the first few weeks I had to get it needled before games, and then it started to settle down. But then I tried to do some training in the off season, and it was just causing me a bit of trouble.

Advertisement

“I’m glad I’ve got that done, so I can go into the season fully fit.” As the Titans contemplate their Grant raid, their state rivals the Dolphins have been dealt a blow tipped to send them to the market for front row reinforcements, after the North Queensland Cowboys confirmed they had snared Thomas Flegler from 2028. Dolphins prop Tom Flegler. Getty Images Flegler – who returned from nearly two years sidelined with nerve damage in his shoulder this year – started for the Maroons in all three State of Origin games in 2026. Now, he looms as the Cowboys’ engine room leader to succeed Jason Taumalolo, who is entering the final year of his 10-season contract. “At 27 his best football is still in front of him and that is going to be played in Cowboys colours,” Cowboys list and recruitment manager Clint Zammit said.

Advertisement

“It is a testament to Tom’s character to not only play rugby league again after such a serious injury, but immediately return and play at a high level.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. title: Rawiller ready to right the wrong in Gong after shattering loss
text:
Advertisement

SportRacingHorse racing Rawiller ready to right the wrong in Gong after shattering loss Craig Kerry November 20, 2026 — 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Nash Rawiller is desperate to help make up for an injustice last time out with Gringotts when the Ciaron Maher-trained star chases a hat-trick of titles in the $1 million The Gong (1600m) at Kembla on Saturday. And the in-form veteran hopes to keep any drama this time on the track. Nash Rawiller celebrates his epic win on Gringotts in the Gong last year. Getty Images After walking the heavy surface, Rawiller took Gringotts to a spine-tingling win in the Gong last year when bucking the trend on a rain-soaked day with an inside run as most jockeys searched wide for better ground. The now seven-year-old has not won since the thrilling half-length victory over Estadio Mestalla, but looked a sure thing beaten in the $3 million Big Dance (1600m) last start.

Advertisement

From gate eight, Rawiller had the favourite midfield in the pack and ready to pounce before they were checked by Formal Display near the 600m mark and lost lengths. Gringotts recovered, only to hit traffic late and finish fourth. Formal Display edged out stablemate Hellsing across the line before Rawiller won a protest against the winner for the interference on the corner, relegating it to fourth and putting Gringotts into third. Gringotts goes to the line behind Hellsing and Formal Display in the Big Dance on November 3 at Randwick. Getty Images The stewards’ room success was small consolation for Rawiller, who apologised to Formal Display’s co-trainer Rob Archibald and jockey Chad Schofield after the decision. “It’s just a shame because I felt like for everyone involved, including the punters, I had to have a throw at the stumps,” Rawiller said.

Advertisement

“To be honest, when I won it, I walked out less flat, because whatever happens, happens, but to take a $3 million race off another set of connections wasn’t great fun really. It had to be done, it’s part of the business, but it wasn’t ideal.” Rawiller welcomed an ideal draw in gate two for Saturday as he looked for better luck with the $2.15 (TAB) favourite, which carries topweight of 61 kilograms. “For me, hopefully we can get it right and make up for what the horse deserves because it was pretty shattering last time,” he said. “I didn’t have a bad day, I left with a couple of winners, but I was pretty flat. One of my favourite horses, and it just felt like a bit of an injustice. “But the horse is terrific, I’ve ridden him in work since. He pulled up like he hadn’t had a run, which, apart from getting flattened, he hadn’t had a run because I hardly let him off the bridle.

Advertisement

“He’s in good form and I think the draw is a huge thing because it null-and-voids the big weight, hopefully. I’ll just have him where he’s comfortable, hopefully a position in the first five, and he gets his chance to let down.” The handy draw gives Rawiller options to ride Gringotts more aggressively, but he was leaning towards a stalking position. Nash Rawiller on Gringotts last year in the Gong. Getty Images “I’ve ridden him more forward on occasions and I just feel he’s not quite as explosive,” he said. “He loves that bit of a suck where he’s sitting just off the speed, and then he can really let down with a great turn of foot.

Advertisement

“But in saying that, he’s very adaptable and if there’s no speed on, I wouldn’t be shy to take up the lead either. But I think in these sorts of races, with big fields, there’s usually speed. “He’s obviously the best horse in the race, but you still need luck to go your way.” Although unlikely to see a repeat of last year’s steady rain, there is a medium chance of showers on the day, which could again lead to a late search for a tactical advantage. “That doesn’t matter,” Rawiller said. “I hope there is, I’ll find it.”

Advertisement

The champion hoop, who turns 52 next month, has been in vintage form, regularly racking up city doubles, including the Five Diamonds-Golden Gift haul at Rosehill two weeks ago. On Friday, he had 28 NSW metropolitan wins at a strike rate of 21.1 per cent to sit third on the premiership behind Zac Lloyd (39) and James McDonald (34). Related Article Horse racing Sherry toasts Big Dance win after protest denies red-hot Schofield He could build on that on Saturday with a strong book featuring Le Chocolat (race one, $6), Congressman (two, $3.80), Crepe Myrtle (four, $7.50), Graffiti Tycoon (five, $1.80), Benevac (six, $4.40) and Ripley (10, $5). “Benevac trialled really well, he’s a nice horse and I think it’s a little bit about getting the first half of the race right with him, and he’s in great order,” Rawiller said. “Graffiti Tycoon is a horse on the way up and I think he will get a bit of confidence out of his win last time.

Advertisement

“He had a nice run off a hot speed. He’s drawn well so he’ll be where he’s comfortable, and hopefully he’ll hit the line again. He’s a big horse who’s still learning how to handle himself, but he’s got upside. “Congressman looks ready to win and I’m not upset about his draw [in 19]. I think he’ll overcome that. “Le Chocolate looks ready to win as well.”

title: Has the RBA gone too far?
text:
Advertisement

BusinessThe economyJobs Opinion Has the RBA gone too far?

November 20, 2026 — 4:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australians have received a barrage of bad economic news lately. Inflation has been stubbornly high, official interest rates have reached an 18-year-high, house prices have slumped and some well-known retailers, including David Jones and General Pants, have collapsed. RBA Governor Michele Bullock during a press conference after the Reserve Bank raised interest rates on November 3. Dominic Lorrimer But perhaps most worrying of all was Thursday’s jobs report from the Australian Bureau of Statistics. It showed the national unemployment rate had jumped from 4.1 per cent in January to a five-year high of 4.9 per cent in October.

Advertisement

Unemployment would have been above 5 per cent if not for an increase in the number of people who gave up looking for work last month. The shock increase did not include major job cuts signalled recently by a raft of big firms, including NAB, ANZ, Qantas, David Jones and Bunnings, so unemployment is set to worsen. Total employment in Australia has already plunged by about 80,000 in the past two months. Rising unemployment is much more than a statistic – it signals an enduring human cost. Since January, the number of people without a job in Australia has surged by 130,000. It now stands at three quarters of a million for the first time since the economic upheaval of the COVID pandemic.

Advertisement

The financial impact of unemployment can be far-reaching and can even affect living standards in retirement. The loss of income for a parent following a job loss may damage the prospects of the next generation. Related Article Analysis

Interest rates One foot in recession: The unemployment numbers that blow up the RBA’s case for hikes An extended period out of work can also damage a person’s wellbeing and sense of self-worth. And of course, higher rates of unemployment damage both federal and state budgets, which are already under pressure. Two aspects of the recent labour market weakness are especially troubling.

Advertisement

First, young workers are being hit disproportionately hard – the youth unemployment rate (for those aged 15 to 24) hit 11.3 per cent in October, the worst in five years. Second, some of the highest unemployment rates in the nation are in parts of Sydney and Melbourne where incomes are relatively low, and many households are already under financial pressure. Regional employment data showed the Parramatta district in Sydney’s west had an unemployment rate of 6.7 per cent in September, while in Melbourne’s west the jobless rate was 6.6 per cent. The meeting’s minutes show that three of the board’s nine members opposed the decision. The sharp rise in unemployment has raised fears Australia is headed for recession – traditionally defined as two consecutive quarters of contraction in national economic output.

Advertisement

Some economists have drawn attention to a recession indicator called the Sahm rule, created by American economist Claudia Sahm. Related Article Australian economy What is a recession and are we in one? A bluffer’s guide Under her definition, a country is on its way to recession if the jobless rate over a three-month period is 0.5 of a percentage point higher than any other three-month period recorded during the preceding year (economists have calculated that this is likely to be about 0.75 of a percentage point in Australia). On Sahm’s measure Australia is skating close to recessionary territory. And yet, only three weeks ago, the Reserve Bank’s monetary policy committee lifted the official cash rate for the fifth time this year in a bid to bring down inflation which, at 4.3 per cent, is still well above the bank’s target band of 2-3 per cent.

Advertisement

The meeting’s minutes show that three of the board’s nine members opposed the decision; the dissenters “expressed their concern that the economy might be near the point of entering a materially sharper downturn and pointed to the costs in terms of unemployment”. The sharp deterioration in the jobs market revealed on Thursday suggests those three dissenters may be right. The Herald is concerned that the Reserve Bank may have lifted rates too high, which will cause unnecessary economic pain. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.
