Australia’s brokers spent another fortnight with their snouts firmly in the trough, as more than $1.4 billion in announced equity packages delivered a feast of heavyweight mandates, chunky commissions and enough broker options to keep one corporate department contemplating knocking off early for Christmas. Canaccord Genuity was busy again, with mandates worth nearly $764 million across uranium, gold and investment-company raisings, while UBS Securities Australia secured a monster $475M mandate without another broker in sight. This edition of Cap Raise Crucible highlights $1 billion raised across 60 companies in the last fortnight However, not every broker needed a nine-figure transaction to make rattling the tin worthwhile. GBA Capital assembled three smaller mandates worth almost $7M, negotiating cash fees and millions of potential broker options. Unfortunate punters had to call for the ambulance, however, with two of its offerings taken to the woodshed, down more than 20 per cent.

Advertisement

And while Capability X and Gorilla Gold both enjoyed spectacular aftermarket runs, nine of the twelve comparable raises and offers traded below issue price, offering plenty of evidence that a discounted placement in the past fortnight was no guarantee of a quick turn. Welcome to this edition of Cap Raise Crucible. Paladin Energy’s Patterson Lake South uranium project in Canada’s Athabasca Basin. PALADIN ENERGY (ASX: PDN) Raised: $525 million, plus proposed $50 million SPP

Issue price: $7.80

Discount: 10.3%

Latest share price: $6.06

Return against issue: -22.3%

Advertisement

Paladin rattled the biggest tin of the fortnight, bagging a whopping $525M in fully underwritten equity to bankroll its Canadian uranium ambitions. And there were enough brokers and bankers around the table to organise a respectable Christmas Day backyard cricket game. Macquarie Capital, Canaccord and RBC Capital Markets shared joint lead-manager, bookrunner and underwriting duties on the Australian portion of the placement, with Shaw and Partners co-managing. RBC and National Bank of Canada Capital Markets handled the Canadian leg of the deal. Investor demand determined the final split, with $499M raised in Australia and around $26M pulled from Canada. The proceeds are slated to support Paladin’s Patterson Lake South development planning, its Triple R resource and mine-life work and the company’s Athabasca exploration, along with general debt reduction.

Advertisement

Punters were offered a handy 10.3 per cent discount to the previous close, which presumably looked attractive when the paperwork landed. Unfortunately, the market soon delivered an even bigger discount. At $6.06, subscribers are already sporting a black eye, nursing a 22.3 per cent loss on their investment. A fully underwritten blockbuster, a roomful of investment bankers popping corks and a share price now suggesting the celebratory ice-cold champers the punters expected was already flat, left out in the sun and well past its best. SERVICE STREAM (ASX: SSM)

Advertisement

Raised: $475 million

Issue price: $2.03

Discount: 7.7%

Latest share price: $1.955

Return against issue: -3.7% While Paladin invited half the broking fraternity to dinner, Service Stream took a rather different approach. UBS landed sole lead-manager, bookrunner and underwriting duties on a hefty $475M equity package supporting the $975M acquisition of infrastructure provider, Programmed. The deal comprised a $219M placement and a $256M accelerated entitlement offer pitched at $2.03, representing a 7.7 per cent discount to the previous close. Unlike Paladin’s first eleven cricket team, UBS had the main equity mandate all to itself.

Advertisement

Service Stream also arranged debt funding as part of the acquisition, although that financing stays outside the Crucible’s equity tally. More importantly for subscribers, the shares finished at $1.955, leaving them just 3.7 per cent below their $2.03 entry price. Punters were not quite eating a fillet steak dinner, but they certainly weren’t hugging the porcelain after a dodgy vindaloo either. Gorilla Gold’s Comet Vale gold project, part of its North Kalgoorlie hub, 100 kilometres north of Kalgoorlie in WA. GORILLA GOLD MINES (ASX: GG8)

Advertisement

Raised: $60 million

Issue price: 26.5c

Discount: Nil; 6% premium to 10-day VWAP

Latest share price: 36.5c

Return against issue: +37.7% If Paladin’s subscribers were wondering where the party had gone, look no further than Gorilla Gold’s shindig, where punters are probably still dancing on the tables. The WA gold explorer secured $60M through Sternship Advisers, BMO Capital Markets and Canaccord as joint lead managers, with Tembo Capital putting a hand in its pocket, stumping up an eye-catching $30M to cornerstone the deal, no doubt helping grease the wheels. Remarkably, the 26.5-cent placement carried zero discount to the previous closing price and was struck six per cent above the 10-day volume-weighted average. You read it right, six per cent above! The proceeds are set to advance Gorilla’s Cosmos, North Kalgoorlie and Vivien gold assets.

Advertisement

The shares touched 40.5 cents last Wednesday, a magnificent 52.8 per cent premium to issue, before easing to 36.5 cents midway through Friday, still leaving punters a handsome 38 per cent ahead. No discount, a substantial institutional book and a post-listing rocket. Somebody clearly remembered to feed the gorilla. Nice work all round! Gorilla’s performance also highlighted the different fortunes awaiting subscribers across Canaccord’s broader collection of mandates. The broker joined Commonwealth Securities, Morgans Financial, Ord Minnett and Taylor Collison on Solaris Australian Equity Income Fund’s package worth up to $91.97M.

Advertisement

That comprised a $28.5M placement and a proposed $63.47M entitlement offer at $2.02; a 5.2 per cent discount to the previous close, although a slight premium to pre-tax net tangible asset backing. At $2.06, placement subscribers were a miserly two per cent ahead, while the entitlement component remains open. It was a considerably more restrained celebration than Gorilla’s party, but still better than the reception awaiting investors in Many Peaks Minerals. Canaccord took the combined global coordinator and sole bookrunner seat on Many Peaks’ $70M placement, sharing joint lead-manager duties with Barrenjoey and SCP Resource Finance. The $1 shares were issued at a 12.3 per cent discount to fund development of the Ferke gold project in Côte d’Ivoire.

Advertisement

Yet despite that sizeable concession, the shares are currently trading at 88 cents, leaving subscribers on the wrong side of the ledger with a 12% loss. Apparently, a double-digit discount is no substitute for an uncooperative share market. The mixed results continued beyond Canaccord’s books. Petra Capital secured lead-manager and sole bookrunner duties on Pacific Lime and Cement’s $50 million placement at 36 cents, with Barrenjoey co-leading and Tamesis Partners co-managing. The proceeds are earmarked for early development work at the company’s cement project near Port Moresby in Papua New Guinea, while Tamesis also advised on a separate prospective financing arrangement.

Advertisement

Subscribers are subsequently 11.1 per cent behind at 32 cents, proving that even a business built around cement could not guarantee a solid aftermarket. Auric Mining’s Burbanks processing facility, subject to a refurbishment study, just 15km from its Union Jack project near Coolgardie. Auric Mining offered a less painful outcome. Canaccord, Taylor Collison and MA Moelis Australia Advisory shared joint lead-manager duties on its $17M placement, with Lazarus Advisory co-managing. The company also proposed a $3M share purchase plan.

Advertisement

The 18.5-cent raise will support work at Auric’s Munda, Union Jack and Iron Maiden projects, alongside potential acquisitions and an upgrade to its Burbanks processing plant. With the shares trading at 17 cents, subscribers’ noses were 8.1 per cent below the waterline. No champagne corks flying, but no need to call the family doctor either. One transaction offering a different flavour involved Western Gold Resources, where the attraction extended beyond the usual institutional placement. Taurus Capital Group took the sole lead-manager role on the $7.5M raising at eight cents, with a disclosed six per cent fee potentially delivering a sweet $450,000 clip on the full amount.

Advertisement

The placement was struck at a 2.6 per cent premium to the previous close and a 6.67 per cent premium to the 15-day VWAP. More interestingly, the highly acquisitive and soon-to-be producing gold miner Forrestania Resources committed $5.5M as a cornerstone investor, strengthening ties around Western Gold’s Gold Duke project and a recent associated ore purchase arrangement. The money is slated to support site establishment, drilling and working capital. Western Gold subsequently finished at 7.4 cents, leaving subscribers 7.5 per cent in the red. Still, Forrestania’s investment was clearly about more than chasing an immediate trading profit. Its strategic relationship gave the deal a dimension missing from many conventional placements.

Advertisement

And then came GBA Capital, which demonstrated that the smaller end of the market could produce some of the more eye-watering broker economics. GBA’s first assignment involved Sarytogan Graphite’s one-for-four entitlement offer seeking up to $3.846M at 5.8 cents - a miserly two per cent below the last closing price - plus a one-for-two, three-year oppy exercisable at 8.7 cents. The broker acted as lead manager and partially underwrote $1M, with remuneration including a $50,000 lead-manager fee, a 1.5 per cent management fee, five per cent underwriting and eligible shortfall-placement fees, plus five options for every dollar of qualifying shortfall placed, on the same terms. The Crucible’s calculator doesn’t have enough memory to do the maths on that one. Our best guess is it’s a pretty penny for underwriting a lazy million, with punters currently seven per cent down on the deal. The funds are destined to support graphite test work and feasibility activities in Kazakhstan, alongside environmental work and copper exploration.

Advertisement

However, an intriguing contrast emerged from GBA’s next two assignments. Northstone Resources raised $2.37M at 0.9 cents to advance its Tlamino gold-silver and Timok East copper projects in Serbia. GBA’s six per cent cash commission amounted to roughly $142,000, with another 26.34M broker options proposed, exercisable at two cents until January 2030, subject to shareholder approval. A tidy incentive for the broker to man the phones. For the hard-bitten thrill-seekers who subscribed, the shares have since tanked 22.2 per cent below the issue price, leaving a trail of blood from injured punters all the way to the emergency department’s door.

Advertisement

GBA then completed its hat-trick with Kuniko Limited’s $600,000 placement at 1.5 cents, collecting another six per cent cash commission worth $36,000. The board also kicked in $80k, usually a good sign. The proposed remuneration included 6.87M listed broker options exercisable at a well out-of-the-money strike price of 7 cents with a May 2029 expiry. Kuniko will use the money for further drilling at its Commonwealth-Silica Hill gold-silver project in NSW. Unfortunately, punters required a stretcher and heavy bandaging, with the shares currently trading at an unsettling 26.7 per cent below issue. Across Northstone and Kuniko alone, GBA’s disclosed cash commissions totalled$178,200, accompanied by 33.2M proposed broker options, subject to shareholder approval. Good luck with that, lads.

Advertisement

Those options may ultimately prove valuable or worthless. Either way, the contrast with the immediate fortunes of their placement subscribers was difficult to ignore. The broker had negotiated its cash remuneration and potential future upside. Some of the punters, meanwhile, had unknowingly been dealt a free option on a visit to ICU. The IPO market supplied one final helping of broker economics, though, when AI-focused Capability X made its ASX debut on November 12 after raising $12M at 20 cents. The company will deploy the proceeds to expand sales, fund research and development, hire technical talent and commercialise its artificial intelligence-driven industrial safety technology. Westar Capital acted as lead manager, with a six per cent fee worth $720,000 and a juicy $10,000 monthly corporate-advisory retainer extending over two years.

Advertisement

The handsome package also included 12M lead-manager options exercisable at 30 cents over three years. But punters won’t begrudge Westar its share of the spoils after Capability X rocketed to 31 cents on debut, a whopping 55 per cent above its 20-cent issue price, before easing to 27.5 cents. With a 37.5 per cent paper profit already in the bag, punters were grinning from ear to ear. Great work, captain. The drinks are on you! Meanwhile, in the good old USA... Wall Street’s AI feeding frenzy reached fever pitch overnight as Claude creator Anthropic stormed onto the Nasdaq in an eye-watering US$81.3 billion (A$122B) IPO. Priced at US$83 (A$124.70), the shares rocketed nearly 39 per cent on debut to US$115.10 (A$173). The stock eventually settled at US$97.17 (A$146), still a handsome 17 per cent premium and valuing the AI heavyweight at roughly US$1.76 trillion (A$2.64T). Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley led a veritable army of investment bankers into the deal, with the underwriting syndicate pocketing a coffee-spitting US$550M (A$826M) in fees. Not a bad night’s work for the corporate suits. Who said the AI market was in trouble? And so, another fortnight drew to a close with brokers pocketing their commissions, underwriting fees and potential option windfalls, while subscribers experienced everything from Gorilla’s 52.8 per cent gain and Capability X’s 55 per cent triumph to Kuniko’s 26.7 per cent tumble and Paladin’s 22.3 per cent loss.

Advertisement

title: Xi Jinping applauds Anthony Albanese for rebuilding China-Australia relations
text:
in brief Xi Jinping has invited greater cooperation with Australia in areas like agriculture, energy, the green economy and AI.

Anthony Albanese said differences would be discussed "constructively and directly".

Chinese President Xi Jinping is willing to cooperate more with Australia in key industries, telling Prime Minister Anthony Albanese there has been a"comprehensive turnaround" in relations.

Speaking on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Forum (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, Xi Jinping said China was willing to work with Australia to expand cooperation, set aside differences and build on recent improvements in relations, taking the partnership to a new stage of development.

"Since you took office as prime minister in 2022, we have met four times. I think it is fair to say that together we have brought about a comprehensive turnaround in China-Australia relations," Xi said.

title: A data centre chair has rebuked Australians who oppose the energy-hungry facilities

Australia would be "nuts" to back away from digital infrastructure, according to the chair of a major data centre operator, after a community campaign in Victoria derailed one of the major facilities in Melbourne.

title: Why our World War Two-era recession formula 'doesn't speak to reality'
text:
In brief The federal government and Reserve Bank have denied Australia will enter a recession, despite economic pressures.

Some economists endorse unemployment as the best indicator of a recession, with one saying GDP is an outdated measure.

Australian households are facing increasing financial pressure, with interest rates, inflation and unemployment on the rise. Despite the squeeze, Australia isn't expected to enter a recession.

The federal government has denied Australia is heading towards recession, with Treasurer Jim Chalmers naming rising interest rates and the war in Iran as major contributors to mounting economic pressure.

Health and Ageing Minister Mark Butler told Sunrise recent figures "show the pressure the economy is under".

"We're not predicting a recession. The Reserve Bank's not predicting a recession either," he said.

The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) describes a recession as a sustained period of weak or negative growth in gross domestic product (GDP) accompanied by a significant rise in unemployment.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Currently, Australia's GDP is rising, but employment is falling.

Australia's GDP grew to 0.4 per cent in the June 2026 quarter, up from 0.3 per cent in the March quarter — and the national GDP slowed from 2.5 per cent in March to 2.1 per cent in June.

Unemployment hit its highest rate in five years in October, rising to 4.9 per cent – up from 4.1 per cent in January.

There remains no formal economic definition of recession. The RBA refers to a 'technical recession' defined by "two consecutive quarters of negative growth in real GDP".

"Whenever you put technical in front of something, it does kind of give away the fact it's an arbitrary measure that doesn't speak to the reality of what might be going on," Greg Jericho, chief economist at left-wing thinktank The Australia Institute, told SBS News.

However, Jericho warns that Australia's method for defining a recession may be outdated — and thus unable to properly determine one.

Is GDP an appropriate indicator for modern economies?

Jericho said the measure of "two consecutive quarters of negative GDP growth" worked well post-World War Two, when there were "manufacturing economies".

He says Australia is now a "service economy" which relies heavily on mining and mining exports.

If an international company exports mined resources from Australia, those exports count towards the nation's GDP figures, Jericho said.

However, the industry doesn't have a high employment rate.

According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics' Labour Force Survey from February 2026, 314,500 Australians work directly in the mining industry — 2.1 per cent of the national workforce.

"So, Australia may have exported a lot of iron ore in one quarter, which helped us stay out of recession, but you or I don't necessarily get any money from iron ore," he said.

The artificial intelligence industry is similar.

"The GDP might be fine because we have the AI investment boom, but it's not providing many jobs, no more income, and it's certainly not driving wage growth," Jericho said.

"It might take us out of that technical recession — but who cares?"

Another issue with a GDP-based assessment of recession is that it's "woefully slow" and GDP figures are often revised, Jericho said.

He said data from two quarters isn't confirmed until "six months after the fact".

Jericho said the GDP is "quite divorced from what people are feeling".

"During the global financial crisis, we didn't have two quarters of consecutive GDP growth, but the unemployment rate rose very quickly — over a percentage point in a year," he said.

"People would have felt very much like it was a recession."

He said Australia's Reserve Bank has "consistently" misread the economy this year.

"They were expecting unemployment to hit 4.9 per cent in December next year ... Three months ago, they thought unemployment by now would be just 4.5 per cent," he said.

"It really highlights that their belief that the economy needs to be slowed by more rate rises was completely wrong."

An employment-based definition?

Former US Federal Reserve economist Claudia Sahm coined the Sahm rule, which says a recession starts when the three-month moving average of the national unemployment rate rises by 0.5 percentage points or more above its lowest level over the prior 12 months.

"By her measure, Australia is pretty much right there," Jericho said.

He said that using Sahm's rule is a proactive option.

Jericho said if unemployment is rising by more than half a per cent in a year, it "keeps going up pretty fast and later lines up with GDP going backwards".

He said acting quickly to address unemployment is crucial to reversing recession.

AMP chief economist Shane Oliver said the October labour force data would be the start of an upward trend in unemployment.

"It's probably a sign of things to come," he told Australian Associated Press.

"The number of job losses reported ... reflect the slowdown in the economy on the back of rate hikes, cost-of-living pressures, poor confidence and so on."

Oliver said the rise was a sign the Reserve Bank's five interest rate hikes in 2026 had worked their way through the economy.

But the moves to slow inflation had led to higher unemployment, which in turn boosted the chances of a recession.

"I'd say the risk is high. It's around 40 per cent," he said.

Jericho maintains that Australia hasn't entered a recession yet. But if unemployment reaches 5 per cent, it would be "really hard to argue that we're not".

The Reserve Bank earlier in November revised its unemployment forecast for the jobless rate to reach five per cent by 2028.

Independent economist Saul Eslake said that figure was more likely to be reached early in 2027.

"These numbers, for the time being at least, further downplay the likelihood of another increase in interest rates in December, and arguably also reduce the probability of another rate hike in February," he said.

October inflation data, due to be released on Wednesday, is likely to confirm the next move by the Reserve Bank's board.

Eslake said future unemployment numbers could be a harbinger of a recession.

— With reporting by the Australian Associated Press

title: Anthropic's epic $3 trillion debut fails to revive flagging investor confidence in AI
text:
In brief Investors have turned sceptical over concerns about the enormous spending needed to build out the sector.

The Nvidia scandal has softened some of the exuberance for the Anthropic listing.

Anthropic's market value has hit a high of $US2.1 trillion ($3.1 trillion) in its Nasdaq debut, soaring past SpaceX's June launch as investors rushed to buy shares of the world's ‌first publicly traded frontier AI company.

The early exuberance, however, partly faded as the main indexes retreated as the super-sized initial public offering (IPO) had failed to revive faded enthusiasm over AI.

The stock opened at $US111.50, some 34 per cent higher than the IPO price of $US83. But the stock pared its gains and was last trading around $99.

The stellar debut caps a turbulent week for the AI sector, marked by Nvidia boss Jensen Huang's scandal-tinged exit, ‌and shifts Wall Street's spotlight on to Anthropic's rival OpenAI as the industry's next major public listing.

Strong demand for Anthropic shares amid a broader tech sell-off offers hope to a sector where euphoria has somewhat cooled in recent weeks.

"Nvidia gave us a read on the build-out, and Anthropic is about to give us a read on investor appetite for the next generation of AI companies."

From economic growth to doomsday warnings

AI technology has boosted economic growth, sparked doomsday warnings and arguably helped usher in a data-centre-sceptic Democratic tsunami in the US mid-term elections.

Investors who once embraced the boom have turned sceptical in recent weeks over concerns the enormous spending needed to build out the sector, and mounting debt loads, may not be justified by the eventual returns.

Anthropic, too, has signalled it may tap debt markets.

"At some point in the ‌future we're hoping to ‌be investment grade, and debt is an ⁠instrument that we have available to us, and we'd like to use at some point in the future," chief executive Dario Amodei told CNBC in an interview.

As the first frontier AI company to go public, Anthropic is poised to become the sector's benchmark, with OpenAI reportedly eyeing a 2027 listing.

Anthropic sold 980 million shares at $US83 ($123) each, pricing the initial public offering (IPO) above its marketed range of $US70 ($103) to $US78 ($115). Its IPO proceeds could climb to as much as $US93.5 billion ($139 billion) if underwriters fully exercise their option to purchase additional shares.

Trillion-dollar club

Anthropic joins the trillion-dollar club alongside Microsoft, Apple and Nvidia.

Although shares can be volatile in the days following a listing, Anthropic's IPO is set to create thousands of paper millionaires and a handful of billionaires,

Based on the IPO price, CEO Amodei and his six co-founders — who together own about 10 per cent of the company — had stakes valued at nearly $US150 billion ($223 billion) combined, according to a calculation based on details in the filing.

More broadly, the listing is expected to create a wave of new wealth across the AI sector, rewarding everyone from early researchers and engineers to administrative staff.

Debate has intensified across global markets in recent months over whether the AI boom is veering into bubble territory, with economists, chief executives and political leaders split over its sustainability.

Much of the scrutiny has focused on circular financing arrangements. A complicated ‌web of deals between AI companies, chipmakers, cloud providers and investors has raised questions over how much of the industry's growth is being fuelled by money circulating within the same ecosystem.

Anthropic's breakneck growth has so far defied these concerns, but some investors have said they may wait for the initial euphoria to subside before buying.

"Anthropic is a one-trick pony," Bill Gunderson, partner at GCG Advisory Partners, said. "People compare it with Amazon because even Amazon lost money for several years, but Anthropic won't have that luxury.

"They've got to get to profitability soon."

title: A rising number of Australians want to go off the grid. What’s it like?
text:
In brief More Australians considered going off-grid as power bills and extreme weather pressures grew.

New research found cost savings and energy independence were key drivers of the shift.

As solar and batteries make it possible for homes to make and store their own power, more Australians are wondering whether they need the power grid at all.

Cost pressures and extreme weather are driving interest. Power prices rose five years in a row before easing this July. One in five Australian households is struggling to pay its energy bills.

Queensland is at the pointy end as the state most exposed to extreme weather. Just last week, a supercell storm left 82,000 residents without power. Last year, ex-tropical Cyclone Alfred left around 250,000 Queenslanders in the dark, some for up to ten days.

Fully 25% of householders in Queensland plan to go off-grid at some point, according to the state’s 2026 energy survey, up from 22% a year earlier. Many have already gone off-grid, especially in regional areas where grid connections can cost tens of thousands of dollars.

But we don’t know much about why Queenslanders make this choice. Once off grid, they become invisible to official data records.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

In our new research, we interviewed off-grid Queenlanders to find out why people do it – and if it’s worth it.

What do off-grid households look like?

Most off-grid households use solar panels to generate power and a home battery to store it. Some keep a backup generator for long cloudy periods.

We surveyed 40 off-grid households, largely located in south-east Queensland. We interviewed ten householders in depth and spoke to four off-grid installers. We also asked utilities and eight councils what their rules say.

Most respondents lived in rural or rural-residential areas. Their homes largely fell into one of two categories:

• Conventional houses (22 households). To go off-grid, the average house had 6.6 kilowatts of solar panels and a 40 kilowatt-hour battery, mostly put in by professional installers.

• Tiny houses on wheels (ten households). These houses had much smaller off-grid systems, averaging about 3.5 kilowatts of solar and two 4 kWh batteries. Some owners installed these themselves and used a licensed electrician to check.

READ MORE The hidden cost of living in Australia's mining heartland

Why do people do it?

The most common motivation was financial, listed by about 55% of survey respondents. But financial reasons meant different things for people in conventional homes and those in tiny homes.

In conventional houses, going off-grid was mostly about avoiding the big cost of grid connection, which can be $30,000 to $60,000.

As one homeowner told us, off-grid meant:

an opportunity to save some money and work towards being self-reliant.

By contrast, going off grid in a tiny house on wheels was seen as part of choosing to live simply. One resident used second-hand solar panels at about $70 per panel. They told us:

I lived in the suburbs, and you’re just getting bills for this, bills for that. [Now] I can buy some stuff, learn how it works, and kind of provide my own energy.

Other motivations included care for the environment (25%), no grid access (20%), independence and control (12.5%) and finally doubts about grid reliability (10%).

The most common complaint (33% of people) was running short of power during long cloudy or rainy periods. But 20% saw no downsides at all.

Many interviewees described feeling more independent and in control of their own energy supply.

Was it worth it?

Off-grid living makes most sense where the power grid is costly to reach or seen as unreliable. Here, a well designed off-grid system can cost the same as, or less than, a grid connection. It comes with the benefit of producing power for free and keeping the lights (and fridge) on in a blackout.

As one participant said:

"My goal was to be self-sufficient […] generating our own power, sourcing our own water and dealing with our own waste. So in other words, I’m not reliant on any of the government utilities."

One downside was the cost of replacement. Household batteries may need to be replaced every ten to 15 years. As another respondent said:

"The return on investment is 20 years and that battery will probably be dead by then."

Only 20% of our respondents went off-grid out of necessity. Almost all the tiny-house residents we spoke with chose this way of living to suit their environmental values.

Streamlining rules makes sense

Off-grid living isn’t for everyone. For suburban households, research shows it’s usually cheaper to add solar but keep the grid connection. Adding a battery as well can bring most of the benefits of going off-grid, such as lower bills and blackout backup, while keeping the grid as insurance.

Going off-grid makes most sense on rural blocks where connection costs are very high, as well as in disaster-prone areas where long blackouts are possible.

The biggest barrier is whether the rules will allow it. It’s often unclear whether a home can disconnect from electricity, let alone water and sewerage. The answer changes from council to council – and energy companies have their own rules on top.

This situation means many householders are uncertain about what they’re legally allowed to do – especially the residents of tiny houses.

Several told us they were flying under the radar and keeping their home out of sight from the road because they weren’t sure their homes were permitted to be there.

To make it viable for more residents, three changes would help:

Make rules consistent state-wide, with clear pathways for both fixed houses and tiny houses on wheels.

Ensure householders can access independent advice so that solar and battery systems are sized properly.

Collect better data on off-grid households so authorities can plan for their needs.

For a growing number of people in Queensland and around Australia, going off-grid is a real choice. Governments should plan for it in their energy and housing policies.

In Miners Rest, a northern suburb of Ballarat, a community group has formed in response to a Resi Ventures data centre development proposal, with organisers expressing concern about its impact on the environment, water supply, fire safety, air quality and electricity.

With Victorians now preparing to vote in the 28 November election, the issue of AI data centres could be key in some electorates.

Victorian state election

In September, the state Labor government laid out new rules for data centre development, including that they would be prohibited in residential zones and would need to be built outside a buffer zone of 150m from homes.

While asserting that data centres "support banking, healthcare, transport and emergency services" the state government said it would "set the rules" in terms of demanding data centre operators use renewable energy supplies, stay away from residential areas, and give back financially to the community.

Victorian Artificial Intelligence Minister Anthony Carbines said companies such as Amazon and Microsoft are investing in Victoria and "that will continue within sensible guardrails".

The Victorian Greens, who have zeroed in on data centres as part of their election campaign and called for a moratorium on all new developments, accused the Labor government of 'scrambling' to rein in the data centres.

"The timing of this backflip says it all. Labor spent the last year trying to turn Victoria into the data centre capital, fast-tracking projects and voting down our moratorium," Sarah Mansfield, Victorian Greens spokesperson for AI and data centres said.

"Now, weeks out from an election and just two days after the Greens led day of action in Footscray supported by hundreds of local community members, they’re scrambling to contain the political mess they created."

Dr Nathan Fioritti, a lecturer in politics from Monash University, told SBS News AI data centres have become an issue for some voters in the upcoming election, which may shift them away from the Labor government and towards parties taking a stand against them.

"Communities and electorates that are affected by this issue are looking to what others are offering. And so in Footscray, there's the Greens' offering, but also the Victorian Socialists have been quite vocal on this as part of their campaign as well. And I expect it will contribute somewhat to the seat potentially becoming winnable for the Greens," Fioritti said.

The Coalition has previously stated data centres should be built in designated precincts, while One Nation proposes banning new developments on prime agricultural land.

Community concerns

Fioritti said there are numerous concerns with data centres, but he believes a primary source of backlash is the lack of community consultation.

"I think that's probably the leading thing, not being consulted properly or not feeling like they had a say in these things without the endorsement or awareness," he said.

Evan Hamman, a research fellow at the Centre for Environmental Governance at the University of Canberra, said the consultation processes communities can participate in for data centre proposals depend on state and local planning frameworks.

READ MORE Australians' shifting attitudes towards this emerging technology revealed

He added that even when data centres pass legal processes, it doesn't necessarily mean they have community approval.

"The point to take away is that regulatory licence is not the same as social licence," Hamman said.

Ideally, Hamman believes, communities facing data centre proposals should be given adequate consultation time, objective information and the "right to get involved in a meaningful way, not a tokenistic way".

Climate Council report

Besides the issue of lack of community consultation, ongoing community concerns about data centres' environmental impacts and impacts on energy costs continue to draw attention, Fioritti said.

Without new renewables and storage to power them, Australia's data centres could push wholesale power prices up 20 per cent across the main grid by 2035, according to a new report from the Climate Council published on Thursday.

The report notes that Australia's nine "dirtiest" data centre proposals could add 40 million tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions a year by 2035 if they do not use renewable power.

Victoria's three data centre proposals would add 17.7 million tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions a year — more than Australia's highest emitting coal power station, Loy Yang A, according to the Climate Council report.

READ MORE A $3 billion downgrade could send a ripple through a surging Australian industry

In August, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced new national rules that would require data centre developers to add more renewable energy to the grid than their data centres consume, minimise water use, and ensure new sites are appropriate for their size — avoiding land that could otherwise be used for housing.

"Australia is in a strong position to attract investment in data centres, but maintaining social licence will be essential," Albanese said.

Future elections

Hamman believes data centres will likely become more of a political flashpoint in Australia in the years to come.

In the US, the overwhelming turn against Republicans in some of the party's heartland states in the recent midterm election was driven in part by opposition to data centres.

"Some of that so-called 'blue wave' was a reponse to data development and an opposition to it," Hamman said.

"What's happened internationally will eventually end up here."

As more large-scale AI data centres are proposed, Hamman believes more Australians will be moved to act on the concerns around them.

He says that newer "so-called hyperscale centres" are going to require a lot more land, a lot more water and energy, and they're going to be a lot more conspicuous in and around where people live.

title: Cameron Bancroft breaks his silence on sandpapergate saga in an explosive column
text:
In brief Cameron Bancroft supported Usman Khawaja's account of the 2018 controversy.

Bancroft said Pat Cummins' comments are at odds with what happened.

Cameron Bancroft has taken aim at Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins in an explosive column about the sandpaper scandal, insisting the whole team knew.

On the same day that Cricket Australia announced an independent forum designed as a "circuit breaker" for the game's crisis, Bancroft went into great detail about the 2018 scandal, its origins and the aftermath.

As the player who used the sandpaper on the ball, Bancroft is a central figure in the saga. He repeatedly states in the lengthy column that Usman Khawaja was right in saying that the whole team knew.

He admitted to not giving a "complete and truthful account" when questioned during Cricket Australia's investigation into what happened during the third Test against South Africa at Newlands.

Bancroft said he is angry at Cummins after his lengthy media conference last Friday, when the paceman and current Test skipper flatly denied Khawaja's claim.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"The final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins' press conference," Bancroft said in the West Australian column.

"It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone.

"What I saw, experienced and lived with — not only him, but everyone else on that tour in South Africa — is not the public account he gave in his press conference and in the years previously when he has spoken on this time.

"In addition to what Usman (Khawaja) already mentioned I have key recollections which affirm what he is saying."

Khawaja and Warner cast doubts on sandpapergate forum

Khawaja and David Warner said they doubt an independent forum created by Cricket Australia will heal all wounds from the sandpaper scandal.

Warner and Khawaja both questioned if the independent forum will find the truth of the controversy — and the CA hierarchy agrees.

"Someone's version of events will contradict someone else's version of events," CA chief executive Todd Greenberg told reporters in Hobart on Wednesday.

"So looking for the perfect truth doesn't exist — and we're not chasing that."

CA wants players and staffers from the infamous 2018 Test tour of South Africa, when Australia tampered with the ball, to tell their version of events to the forum.

"This forum is not about re-litigating the past," CA's interim chairman David Boon told reporters in Hobart on Wednesday.

"It's about creating an opportunity for those who wish to be heard to tell their stories in a respectful, safe environment — and for our sport to listen."

Khawaja, whose recount of the events in his autobiography released last week triggered the fresh furore, applauded CA's board for establishing the forum, but doubted its effectiveness.

"The biggest question I have is ... the board makes the decisions on what comes out at the end," Khawaja told Fox Cricket.

"How is that an actual way of trying to present what people have said? I just feel that then we just go in a circle again.

"I appreciate where their heart is and I will support the board in this ... but for me there are still a few questions."

Warner, who was banned from cricket for 12 months for his role in the sandpaper scheme, concurred.

"This safe space again — is it really going to be safe? Where do we actually end here?" he told Fox Cricket.

Cricket Australia CEO Todd Greenberg announced the forum in Hobart. Source: AAP / James Ross

Greenberg said players and staffers from the time wouldn't be forced to attend the forum, likely to be headed by a King's Counsel and operated entirely independent of CA.

"Over the past week, we have had several different and conflicting accounts of what transpired in Cape Town in 2018," he said.

"And it has been an incredibly difficult and uncomfortable time for the game and for everyone who was involved.

"The game is really hurting at the moment.

"These events were eight years ago. They caused enormous pain and hurt for lots of people, and they're doing it again.

"And at some point we have to move forward, and we can't move forward without putting some of these steps in place."

Greenberg said CA would decide what, if any, outcome from the forum would be released publicly.

"The premise is that they (players and staff) are coming through and it's confidential," he said.

"That (outcome release) will ultimately be a matter for the CA board at the time. And, where possible, we would like to think that we can make as much of that public as we can."

There would not be sanctions for anyone involved in the forum, he said, hoping it would be completed in a month.

And Greenberg again ruled out reopening CA's investigation into the 2018 scandal completed at the time.

Eight of the 11 Australian players who played in the Cape Town Test were interviewed by that investigation, which Warner has described as a botched cover-up.

Khawaja, in his book, said the entire Test touring squad was aware of plans to tamper with the ball.

But current Test captain Pat Cummins, who was in the 2018 team, described Khawaja's claims as nonsense, while dismissing any notion of a masterplan to tamper with the ball.

CA banned Steve Smith, along with Warner, for 12 months and stripped them of the captaincy and vice-captaincy respectively for their role in the controversy.

Bancroft, who was caught by television cameras with sandpaper in his trousers during the Cape Town Test, was suspended for nine months.

Australian investors have received a fraction of the Anthropic shares they applied for, but those who bought into the artificial intelligence company enjoyed a 17 per cent value jump in the first day of trading on Friday. Despite a bad day on the market overall, the Claude-maker’s record-breaking IPO pushed the combined wealth of its seven co-founders to $US166 billion ($249 billion) as shares of the AI lab jumped following its debut. Sydney motor mechanic Nadav didn’t get all the shares he wanted in Anthropic, but was still happy to invest. Dominic Lorrimer The stock, priced at $US83 a share, soared to $US111.50 in early trade, giving the company a market capitalisation of more than $US2 trillion ($3 trillion) in early trade before paring gains. It closed at $US97.17 in New York trading, giving the company a value of about $US1.8 trillion ($2.7 trillion) and valuing each founder’s fortune at about $US24 billion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. The $US107.3 billion public offering and concurrent private placement broke SpaceX’s record for the biggest-ever.

Advertisement

Sydney mechanic Nadav, who declined to provide his surname, said he had received 7 per cent of the shares he had applied for via the online brokerage Stake. “With it being so oversubscribed, the majority of people didn’t get the allocation they were expecting, so I was a bit disappointed,” the 31-year-old said. But overall, he said, it was “exciting to be a part of it”. Some people who attempted to buy shares via other companies reportedly missed out altogether because demand was so strong. It is common for firms listing on the stock market to offer fewer shares than investors would ultimately like to ensure a “pop” in value, which can help to build momentum. After the listing, Nadav said he bought more shares in the company to take his holding up to 10, split between a personal account and superannuation fund. He said he regularly used AI tools, including Anthropic’s Claude, to run his garage and communicate with customers. “It makes sense I want the company to do well,” Nadav said.

Advertisement

Advertisement

Keeping things equal Anthropic has an unusually even ownership structure among its founders, with each holding about the same 1.3 per cent fully diluted economic stake in the firm. Despite their relatively small economic stakes, the founders retain outsized control over the company through Founder LLC, an entity that owns a single Class F share carrying 50.1 per cent of voting power. All seven have pledged to dedicate 80 per cent of their personal company equity to philanthropic causes, but that is not legally binding. A big step for Silicon Valley

Founded in January 2021 by former OpenAI employees, Anthropic was valued at $US461 million in its Series A funding round that year, according to PitchBook. Since then, its valuation has climbed more than 320,000 per cent, based on the fully diluted valuation implied by the offering price. Australian broking services and banks have made access to popular US public listings a point of distinction. On Friday, Stake’s website read “Anthropic has arrived” in bold text. Ashton Kutcher, pictured with wife Mila Kunis, is a big winner from the Anthropic float. Invision/AP Wealth managers Morgans, Bell Potter, LGT Wealth and Morgan Stanley all had access to the IPO in Australia, alongside online brokers Sharesies and CommSec. Jonathan Belz, chief executive of BFA Global Investors, said his firm had put about $30 million into Anthropic for its clients in multiple rounds before the public offering.

“Obviously, we haven’t exited yet, these things have escrow, so victory dances at first day IPO prices may be a little bit premature,” said Belz, whose firm invests on behalf of institutions and wealthy families. Related Article Updated

He said the firm and its bankers appeared to have prioritised investors who could make large commitments, big Anthropic customers, and its business partners. Retail investors have played an increasing role in the success of some technology stocks, including SpaceX, where charismatic founders have developed large fan bases.

The staggering sum of money that investors have poured into AI stocks this year has fuelled fears of a bubble. On Friday, the outgoing chairman of Australian AI data centre developer NextDC, Douglas Flynn, riffed on those worries. “Is it a bubble? Who knows? That is the index’s longest losing streak since 2024. It is down 8.2 per cent from its record set last month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 2.2 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite sank 2.3 per cent. The losses were widespread, and more than 90 per cent of the stocks that make up the S&P 500 fell. There’s only one word to describe markets this week… Carnage. As of mid-market Friday, the ASX is in the midst of its seventh straight losing session, a plunge of more than six per cent that has now wiped out every cent of its 2026 gains. This week’s Bulls N’ Bears ASX Runner of the Week is… Black Rock Mining. It is the worst run since the war kicked off in April, when oil shocks from Iran rocked the market. No doubt traderswould have closed the screens early on Friday and, at this rate, will be closing up shop completely by next week, as a sea of red continues to spread across almost every market and sector. Wall Street has fared no better, shedding around five per cent on the week, with the S&P 500 notching six straight losses and the Dow closing below 50,000 for the first time since June.

Advertisement

2027 can’t come soon enough. With no money to splash about on Christmas presents, the punters would probably be just as happy to hit the reset button on a bottomed-out economy and hope the new year brings a market rebound – and a few dollars back in their pockets to reinvest. Locally, they’re calling it a commod-apocalypse. As the AI trade continued to unravel and weak Chinese economic data added to the gloom this week, copper was the biggest casualty. Dr Copper, the economy’s bellwether, has fallen to US$5.57 a pound from US$6.65 just three weeks ago - 14 per cent - with Wednesday’s plunge its worst single-day fall since Trump tariff pandemonium. China’s October numbers also missed badly across the board, with retail sales growing just 0.4 per cent and investment shrinking 8.1 per cent. The AI sell-off and a flailing superpower in the east have sent jitters through a market increasingly hanging its hopes on data centre demand. Then gold joined the fray. Hawkish Fed minutes, a flight to cash and a surging US dollar sent the precious metal reaching for its emergency parachute. The shiny yellow metal said ‘Hold my beer’ and crashed to US$3525 an ounce by Friday. That’s a crippling seven per cent fall on the week, as Australian gold miners chalked up their own seventh straight session of hell. At this point, it might be better not to open the trading screen at all, to save shielding your eyes from the glowing crimson. AI offered no refuge in the end either. Nvidia posted revenue of US$115.8 billion (A$174 billion), more than double the year before and delivered a forecast above expectations. It still fell for a fifth straight session.

Advertisement

Even Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO couldn’t save the trade. Its blockbuster listing and public and private placements raised a whopping US$107.3 billion (A$161 billion), with Nvidia, Microsoft, Google and AMD all chipping in. The company briefly hit a US$2 trillion valuation on opening – more than SpaceX – before the broader sell-off dragged it back down too. Back home, Dr Jim Chalmers’ economy shed 44,000 jobs last month, pushing unemployment to 4.9 per cent - a five-year high - prompting headlines to declare what Runners had suggested seven weeks ago: Australia has one foot firmly in the recession bucket. After five rate hikes in seven meetings, government-induced inflation has done what everyone but the Labor government seemed to know it would: kill productivity and choke growth. Meanwhile, at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, the world’s leader Trump, Xi and even Putin held their first-ever three-way meeting, which unfortunately appeared to achieve little after Trump left early. Albo, who wasn’t in the room for that one, did get a moment of his own to tell Putin to end his war in Ukraine, after Australians broadly criticised the Prime Minister for posing for a group photo alongside the Russian president. On a week when almost the entire ASX was begging for the closing bell, only a handful of stocks managed to swim against the tide. A couple of small-cap miners, a pharmaceutical heavyweight and some spectacular gold grades were enough to earn a place among this week’s Runners. They managed to keep their heads above water for most of the week, before even the green shoots – bar a few in healthcare – were swallowed by the market sell-off on Friday. Black Rock Mining is pushing ahead with early works at its giant Mahenge graphite project in Tanzania after securing fresh funding.

Advertisement

BLACK ROCK MINING LTD (ASX: BKT) Up 125% (0.8c – 1.8c) Bulls N’ Bears Runner of the Week is Black Rock Mining, which surged after securing fresh funding in Tanzania to push ahead with early works at its giant Mahenge graphite project in the country’s south. The company says it has secured a US$5 million (A$7.5 million) early drawdown from Tanzanian bank CRDB, giving it the cash to mobilise contractors to site ahead of earthworks before the wet season arrives. It is a practical step towards construction, with Black Rock looking to have the groundwork in place for a rapid transition once the remaining financing is secured and a final investment decision is handed down, projected for early in the new year.

Advertisement

The company says plenty is happening on the funding front. Black Rock has reaffirmed a conditional US$40 million (A$60 million) equity commitment from South Korean industrial giant POSCO International and inked a non-binding deal with African Critical Minerals for a proposed US$70 million (A$105 million) cornerstone investment. Backed by South Africa’s Public Investment Corporation and Lionhead Capital Advisors, the proposed investment would help bankroll the first stage of Mahenge. Combined with existing debt and prepayment facilities, the various funding arrangements now account for US$258 million of the roughly US$298 million required for Module 1, leaving just US$40 million (A$60 million) to close the gap. Mahenge itself is no small operation, boasting a 213.1-million-tonne resource grading 7.8 per cent total graphitic carbon, including a 70.5-million-tonne ore reserve at 8.5 per cent. Its access to Tanzania’s hydro-dominated electricity grid is a key development advantage, with competitively priced power key to keeping operating costs in the lowest-cost quartile. The next pre-final investment decision phase is expected to include further front-end engineering design and tendering for the transmission line contracts, as PowerPoint plans turn to foundations on the ground. With contractors preparing to mobilise and most of the initial funding requirement now identified, Black Rock is edging closer to the big one: financial close and a construction decision.

Advertisement

MAYNE PHARMA GROUP LTD (ASX: MYX) Up 85% ($3.30 - $6.10) Snagging silver on the Runners podium and back dominating the headlines this week was Aussie pharmaceutical manufacturer Mayne Pharma Group, after agreeing to a $604 million cash takeover by the $10 billion-plus Hungarian pharmaceutical heavyweight Gedeon Richter. The takeover offered $6.40 a share, representing a whopping 99.4 per cent premium to its previous closing price and124 per cent above the 30-day volume-weighted average price for the languishing South Australian manufacturer. Richter has operations in roughly 50 countries and says Mayne’s established US commercial presence and product portfolio is the perfect platform to expand its women’s health business globally.

Advertisement

Mayne’s board has unanimously backed the deal, subject to the usual conditions and no superior proposal emerging. But there is plenty of fine print. The scheme is conditional on Mayne completing the sale of its international business to Evaris, while Richter has an exit provision if Mayne’s underlying EBITDA falls by more than $12 million in the current financial year. That is worth keeping an eye on, given Mayne generated $34.2 million in EBITDA last year. The deal also comes with a sizeable dose of déjà vu. In February last year, US-based Cosette Pharmaceuticals agreed to buy Mayne for $7.40 a share, valuing the company at about $672 million. That deal descended into a legal stoush after Cosette sought to walk away, alleging a material adverse change in Mayne’s earnings and sales performance. Mayne took the fight to the NSW Supreme Court; however, the deal was ultimately blocked by Federal Treasurer Jim Chalmers on national interest grounds, with concerns raised about local jobs, critical medical supply chains and Mayne’s long-standing Adelaide manufacturing facility. The Cosette saga ended in December, leaving shareholders back at square one. This time around, the proposed Richter transaction does not require FIRB approval, although the sale of Mayne’s international arm remains subject to its own approvals.

Advertisement

For shareholders who have endured the previous takeover drama, a cash offer at a hefty premium will no doubt be welcome. But with conditions still to be satisfied, the paperwork not quite finished, it’s doubtful long-term holders will be celebrating early. A drill rig on site at Metal Hawk’s Numbat prospect within its broader Leinster South project in WA. METAL HAWK LIMITED (ASX: MHK) Up 62% (13c – 21c) Rounding out this week’s Runners podium is WA gold explorer Metal Hawk, which has struck grades capable of making even the most battered gold market this week sit up and take notice.

Advertisement

The company says it delivered its richest gold results yet from the emerging Numbat shear discovery at the company’s Leinster South project, including a spectacular 11-metre hit grading 48.3 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 103m, featuring a blistering six-metre run at 81.2g/t. That sort of grade tends to cut through even the ugliest market sell-off and could even make the US$500-an-ounce gold prices of the 20th century look positively palatable. There is also serious thickness behind it, with other holes returning 4m at 28.5g/t and a broader 27m at 5.7g/t from the project’s south, at its Thylacine area. Metal Hawk says its latest 11-metre intersection sits 60m further down-plunge from its initial discovery holes, with hopes the structure could be strengthening and even emerging into a much bigger gold system with room to grow. What makes the results particularly interesting is where the gold is turning up. Earlier exploration had largely focused on the quartz veins at Numbat, where the richest mineralisation is usually found. However, the latest drilling has repeatedly returned gold from the surrounding sheared dolerite and gabbro, with significant intersections in every hole drilled beneath the earlier shear discovery. In other words, the quartz lode may only be part of the story. Metal Hawk is now investigating whether the surrounding sheared rocks host a much broader gold-bearing system, rather than being confined to a narrow run of high-grade quartz.

Advertisement

Leinster South sits in one of WA’s established gold districts, with major operators surrounding the junior explorer and plenty of regional mining infrastructure nearby. That is a handy postcode for any discovery, particularly if Metal Hawk can demonstrate that the Numbat mineralisation has the continuity and scale to attract a bigger audience. The company has already extended its diamond drilling campaign to follow up the latest results and test the broader system. Gold prices may be having a rough trot, but grades of 81.2g/t across handy widths tend to do their own talking, no matter how ugly the market gets. Analysis SportNRLNRL 2026 These subtle ploys proved Grant is the best. But is he what the Titans need? Nick Wright November 20, 2026 — 5:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. There are few, if any, who can manipulate a ruck quite like Harry Grant – his exploits in helping deliver another Rugby League World Cup triumph to Australia highlighting that, and adding weight to the Titans’ pursuit of the star hooker. But Gold Coast five-eighth Jayden Campbell has stressed that as much as Grant would add to a young and developing roster, assurances needed to be made that he – and any other prospective recruits – would be arriving at the Glitter Strip for the sole purpose of delivering glory to a region which has been deprived of it. “I’ve grown up on the Gold Coast, the Gold Coast has looked after me and my family, and I just want to give back to the Titans and bring success to the Titans,” Campbell said. Harry Grant is a man in demand, however the Titans have downplayed a pursuit publicly, with chief executive Steve Mitchell saying “There are probably 17 clubs who are going ‘is it worth having a chat to Harry?’” Getty Images “I want people at the Titans for the right reasons and to win as well, I’m not saying anyone doesn’t, but hopefully people come for the right reasons and see we’re on the up.”

Advertisement

The Titans have a history of making big money moves in recruitment to no avail – Jarryd Hayne, Shannon Boyd and David Fifita among those whose careers went downhill at the club. But Grant would be a different beast. Grant was instrumental in the Kangaroos’ 32-12 triumph of New Zealand at Suncorp Stadium’s World Cup final, orchestrating the way his side overcame their size disadvantage in the forward pack by exploiting tired markers and putting the likes of Cameron Munster and Jacob Preston into space behind the ruck. His deception laid on the first try of the night within 85 seconds when he faked to his left and fired a pass for Liam Martin to his right. The 28-year-old’s identification of weary defenders was on show earlier in the semi-final against Samoa when he set up Reece Walsh. Grant maintained he would delay contract talks until after the World Cup, having not taken a player option in his favour for 2028 with Melbourne. He is expected to command north of $1 million a season, and will have no shortage of options on the open market; with some reports suggesting he could seek a lifestyle change.

Advertisement

A feather in the Gold Coast’s cap could be his close relationship with minority owner Matthew Johns. Campbell appreciated the role Grant could play in educating a squad short on experience, and a spine consisting of himself, Zane Harrison (aged 20) and Keano Kini (22). The club – who have played just two finals games in the past 16 seasons – is also expected to lean on their junior talent in the forward pack; Arama Hau and Bodhi Sharpley set for more responsibility alongside Tino Fa’asuamaleaui, Moeaki Fotuaika and Beau Fermor.

Advertisement

But the son of club legend Preston Campbell – who shared similar sentiments with this masthead – believed the Titans had strong No.9 options in Oliver Pascoe and emerging teenager Jai Bilish, and a push for Grant’s signature needed to be fuelled by the dummy-half’s premiership desire; which Grant alluded in the build up to Sunday’s World Cup decider. “It’d be silly for any club to not look at Harry Grant – look at the type of player he is, and what he’s done in the game so far. But we’ve got a really good hooker in Ollie at our club now, he was one of our best players last year,” Campbell said. Jayden Campbell knows how valuable Harry Grant could be, but wants assurance a potential move would be to benefit the club more than a lifestyle change. “Having someone like Harry Grant at any club would be great, but what we’ve got now I’m really happy with, and I’m sure the coaching staff are happy with. We’ve got Ollie and Jai Bilish coming through, so no disrespect to any player or anything, but I’m really happy with what we’ve got, and we just want to work with what we’ve got now.” His father Preston added earlier: “If we can maintain that spine and the boys get to play alongside each other and get to understand each other a little bit more, we’re going to start seeing some more wins.”

Advertisement

Related Article Analysis

NRL 2026 The new face, the student and the veteran: The battle to succeed Reynolds Campbell has cast his eye on building on his fledgling halves combination with Harrison, as he revealed he spent the latter stages of 2026 playing through injury. Campbell said he would begin his preseason continuing his rehabilitation, but was aiming to be training in full after Christmas ahead of the Gold Coast’s maiden appearance in Las Vegas for round one. “I had to get my knee cleaned out at the end of the year, and then I was dealing with a turf toe injury at the back of the year, and it ended up being a few ligaments and a few cracked bones,” Campbell said. “I was playing with it for about eight weeks, the first few weeks I had to get it needled before games, and then it started to settle down. But then I tried to do some training in the off season, and it was just causing me a bit of trouble.

Advertisement

“I’m glad I’ve got that done, so I can go into the season fully fit.” As the Titans contemplate their Grant raid, their state rivals the Dolphins have been dealt a blow tipped to send them to the market for front row reinforcements, after the North Queensland Cowboys confirmed they had snared Thomas Flegler from 2028. Dolphins prop Tom Flegler. Getty Images Flegler – who returned from nearly two years sidelined with nerve damage in his shoulder this year – started for the Maroons in all three State of Origin games in 2026. Now, he looms as the Cowboys’ engine room leader to succeed Jason Taumalolo, who is entering the final year of his 10-season contract. “At 27 his best football is still in front of him and that is going to be played in Cowboys colours,” Cowboys list and recruitment manager Clint Zammit said.

Advertisement

“It is a testament to Tom’s character to not only play rugby league again after such a serious injury, but immediately return and play at a high level.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. title: Rawiller ready to right the wrong in Gong after shattering loss
text:
Advertisement

SportRacingHorse racing Rawiller ready to right the wrong in Gong after shattering loss Craig Kerry November 20, 2026 — 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Nash Rawiller is desperate to help make up for an injustice last time out with Gringotts when the Ciaron Maher-trained star chases a hat-trick of titles in the $1 million The Gong (1600m) at Kembla on Saturday. And the in-form veteran hopes to keep any drama this time on the track. Nash Rawiller celebrates his epic win on Gringotts in the Gong last year. Getty Images After walking the heavy surface, Rawiller took Gringotts to a spine-tingling win in the Gong last year when bucking the trend on a rain-soaked day with an inside run as most jockeys searched wide for better ground. The now seven-year-old has not won since the thrilling half-length victory over Estadio Mestalla, but looked a sure thing beaten in the $3 million Big Dance (1600m) last start.

Advertisement

From gate eight, Rawiller had the favourite midfield in the pack and ready to pounce before they were checked by Formal Display near the 600m mark and lost lengths. Gringotts recovered, only to hit traffic late and finish fourth. Formal Display edged out stablemate Hellsing across the line before Rawiller won a protest against the winner for the interference on the corner, relegating it to fourth and putting Gringotts into third. Gringotts goes to the line behind Hellsing and Formal Display in the Big Dance on November 3 at Randwick. Getty Images The stewards’ room success was small consolation for Rawiller, who apologised to Formal Display’s co-trainer Rob Archibald and jockey Chad Schofield after the decision. “It’s just a shame because I felt like for everyone involved, including the punters, I had to have a throw at the stumps,” Rawiller said.

Advertisement

“To be honest, when I won it, I walked out less flat, because whatever happens, happens, but to take a $3 million race off another set of connections wasn’t great fun really. It had to be done, it’s part of the business, but it wasn’t ideal.” Rawiller welcomed an ideal draw in gate two for Saturday as he looked for better luck with the $2.15 (TAB) favourite, which carries topweight of 61 kilograms. “For me, hopefully we can get it right and make up for what the horse deserves because it was pretty shattering last time,” he said. “I didn’t have a bad day, I left with a couple of winners, but I was pretty flat. One of my favourite horses, and it just felt like a bit of an injustice. “But the horse is terrific, I’ve ridden him in work since. He pulled up like he hadn’t had a run, which, apart from getting flattened, he hadn’t had a run because I hardly let him off the bridle.

Advertisement

“He’s in good form and I think the draw is a huge thing because it null-and-voids the big weight, hopefully. I’ll just have him where he’s comfortable, hopefully a position in the first five, and he gets his chance to let down.” The handy draw gives Rawiller options to ride Gringotts more aggressively, but he was leaning towards a stalking position. Nash Rawiller on Gringotts last year in the Gong. Getty Images “I’ve ridden him more forward on occasions and I just feel he’s not quite as explosive,” he said. “He loves that bit of a suck where he’s sitting just off the speed, and then he can really let down with a great turn of foot.

Advertisement

“But in saying that, he’s very adaptable and if there’s no speed on, I wouldn’t be shy to take up the lead either. But I think in these sorts of races, with big fields, there’s usually speed. “He’s obviously the best horse in the race, but you still need luck to go your way.” Although unlikely to see a repeat of last year’s steady rain, there is a medium chance of showers on the day, which could again lead to a late search for a tactical advantage. “That doesn’t matter,” Rawiller said. “I hope there is, I’ll find it.”

Advertisement

The champion hoop, who turns 52 next month, has been in vintage form, regularly racking up city doubles, including the Five Diamonds-Golden Gift haul at Rosehill two weeks ago. On Friday, he had 28 NSW metropolitan wins at a strike rate of 21.1 per cent to sit third on the premiership behind Zac Lloyd (39) and James McDonald (34). Related Article Horse racing Sherry toasts Big Dance win after protest denies red-hot Schofield He could build on that on Saturday with a strong book featuring Le Chocolat (race one, $6), Congressman (two, $3.80), Crepe Myrtle (four, $7.50), Graffiti Tycoon (five, $1.80), Benevac (six, $4.40) and Ripley (10, $5). “Benevac trialled really well, he’s a nice horse and I think it’s a little bit about getting the first half of the race right with him, and he’s in great order,” Rawiller said. “Graffiti Tycoon is a horse on the way up and I think he will get a bit of confidence out of his win last time.

Advertisement

“He had a nice run off a hot speed. He’s drawn well so he’ll be where he’s comfortable, and hopefully he’ll hit the line again. He’s a big horse who’s still learning how to handle himself, but he’s got upside. “Congressman looks ready to win and I’m not upset about his draw [in 19]. I think he’ll overcome that. “Le Chocolate looks ready to win as well.”

title: Has the RBA gone too far?
text:

BusinessThe economyJobs Opinion Has the RBA gone too far?

November 20, 2026 — 4:52pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Australians have received a barrage of bad economic news lately. Inflation has been stubbornly high, official interest rates have reached an 18-year-high, house prices have slumped and some well-known retailers, including David Jones and General Pants, have collapsed. RBA Governor Michele Bullock during a press conference after the Reserve Bank raised interest rates on November 3. Dominic Lorrimer But perhaps most worrying of all was Thursday’s jobs report from the Australian Bureau of Statistics. It showed the national unemployment rate had jumped from 4.1 per cent in January to a five-year high of 4.9 per cent in October.

Advertisement

Unemployment would have been above 5 per cent if not for an increase in the number of people who gave up looking for work last month. The shock increase did not include major job cuts signalled recently by a raft of big firms, including NAB, ANZ, Qantas, David Jones and Bunnings, so unemployment is set to worsen. Total employment in Australia has already plunged by about 80,000 in the past two months. Rising unemployment is much more than a statistic – it signals an enduring human cost. Since January, the number of people without a job in Australia has surged by 130,000. It now stands at three quarters of a million for the first time since the economic upheaval of the COVID pandemic.

Advertisement

The financial impact of unemployment can be far-reaching and can even affect living standards in retirement. The loss of income for a parent following a job loss may damage the prospects of the next generation. Related Article Analysis

Interest rates One foot in recession: The unemployment numbers that blow up the RBA’s case for hikes An extended period out of work can also damage a person’s wellbeing and sense of self-worth. And of course, higher rates of unemployment damage both federal and state budgets, which are already under pressure. Two aspects of the recent labour market weakness are especially troubling.

Advertisement

First, young workers are being hit disproportionately hard – the youth unemployment rate (for those aged 15 to 24) hit 11.3 per cent in October, the worst in five years. Second, some of the highest unemployment rates in the nation are in parts of Sydney and Melbourne where incomes are relatively low, and many households are already under financial pressure. Regional employment data showed the Parramatta district in Sydney’s west had an unemployment rate of 6.7 per cent in September, while in Melbourne’s west the jobless rate was 6.6 per cent. The meeting’s minutes show that three of the board’s nine members opposed the decision. The sharp rise in unemployment has raised fears Australia is headed for recession – traditionally defined as two consecutive quarters of contraction in national economic output.

Advertisement

Some economists have drawn attention to a recession indicator called the Sahm rule, created by American economist Claudia Sahm. Related Article Australian economy What is a recession and are we in one? A bluffer’s guide Under her definition, a country is on its way to recession if the jobless rate over a three-month period is 0.5 of a percentage point higher than any other three-month period recorded during the preceding year (economists have calculated that this is likely to be about 0.75 of a percentage point in Australia). On Sahm’s measure Australia is skating close to recessionary territory. And yet, only three weeks ago, the Reserve Bank’s monetary policy committee lifted the official cash rate for the fifth time this year in a bid to bring down inflation which, at 4.3 per cent, is still well above the bank’s target band of 2-3 per cent.

Advertisement

The meeting’s minutes show that three of the board’s nine members opposed the decision; the dissenters “expressed their concern that the economy might be near the point of entering a materially sharper downturn and pointed to the costs in terms of unemployment”. The sharp deterioration in the jobs market revealed on Thursday suggests those three dissenters may be right. The Herald is concerned that the Reserve Bank may have lifted rates too high, which will cause unnecessary economic pain. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.
