Australia’s brokers spent another fortnight with their snouts firmly in the trough, as more than $1.4 billion in announced equity packages delivered a feast of heavyweight mandates, chunky commissions and enough broker options to keep one corporate department contemplating knocking off early for Christmas. Canaccord Genuity was busy again, with mandates worth nearly $764 million across uranium, gold and investment-company raisings, while UBS Securities Australia secured a monster $475M mandate without another broker in sight. This edition of Cap Raise Crucible highlights $1 billion raised across 60 companies in the last fortnight However, not every broker needed a nine-figure transaction to make rattling the tin worthwhile. GBA Capital assembled three smaller mandates worth almost $7M, negotiating cash fees and millions of potential broker options. Unfortunate punters had to call for the ambulance, however, with two of its offerings taken to the woodshed, down more than 20 per cent.

Advertisement

And while Capability X and Gorilla Gold both enjoyed spectacular aftermarket runs, nine of the twelve comparable raises and offers traded below issue price, offering plenty of evidence that a discounted placement in the past fortnight was no guarantee of a quick turn. Welcome to this edition of Cap Raise Crucible. Paladin Energy’s Patterson Lake South uranium project in Canada’s Athabasca Basin. PALADIN ENERGY (ASX: PDN) Raised: $525 million, plus proposed $50 million SPP

Issue price: $7.80

Discount: 10.3%

Latest share price: $6.06

Return against issue: -22.3%

Advertisement

Paladin rattled the biggest tin of the fortnight, bagging a whopping $525M in fully underwritten equity to bankroll its Canadian uranium ambitions. And there were enough brokers and bankers around the table to organise a respectable Christmas Day backyard cricket game. Macquarie Capital, Canaccord and RBC Capital Markets shared joint lead-manager, bookrunner and underwriting duties on the Australian portion of the placement, with Shaw and Partners co-managing. RBC and National Bank of Canada Capital Markets handled the Canadian leg of the deal. Investor demand determined the final split, with $499M raised in Australia and around $26M pulled from Canada. The proceeds are slated to support Paladin’s Patterson Lake South development planning, its Triple R resource and mine-life work and the company’s Athabasca exploration, along with general debt reduction.

Advertisement

Punters were offered a handy 10.3 per cent discount to the previous close, which presumably looked attractive when the paperwork landed. Unfortunately, the market soon delivered an even bigger discount. At $6.06, subscribers are already sporting a black eye, nursing a 22.3 per cent loss on their investment. A fully underwritten blockbuster, a roomful of investment bankers popping corks and a share price now suggesting the celebratory ice-cold champers the punters expected was already flat, left out in the sun and well past its best. SERVICE STREAM (ASX: SSM)

Advertisement

Raised: $475 million

Issue price: $2.03

Discount: 7.7%

Latest share price: $1.955

Return against issue: -3.7% While Paladin invited half the broking fraternity to dinner, Service Stream took a rather different approach. UBS landed sole lead-manager, bookrunner and underwriting duties on a hefty $475M equity package supporting the $975M acquisition of infrastructure provider, Programmed. The deal comprised a $219M placement and a $256M accelerated entitlement offer pitched at $2.03, representing a 7.7 per cent discount to the previous close. Unlike Paladin’s first eleven cricket team, UBS had the main equity mandate all to itself.

Advertisement

Service Stream also arranged debt funding as part of the acquisition, although that financing stays outside the Crucible’s equity tally. More importantly for subscribers, the shares finished at $1.955, leaving them just 3.7 per cent below their $2.03 entry price. Punters were not quite eating a fillet steak dinner, but they certainly weren’t hugging the porcelain after a dodgy vindaloo either. Gorilla Gold’s Comet Vale gold project, part of its North Kalgoorlie hub, 100 kilometres north of Kalgoorlie in WA. GORILLA GOLD MINES (ASX: GG8)

Advertisement

Raised: $60 million

Issue price: 26.5c

Discount: Nil; 6% premium to 10-day VWAP

Latest share price: 36.5c

Return against issue: +37.7% If Paladin’s subscribers were wondering where the party had gone, look no further than Gorilla Gold’s shindig, where punters are probably still dancing on the tables. The WA gold explorer secured $60M through Sternship Advisers, BMO Capital Markets and Canaccord as joint lead managers, with Tembo Capital putting a hand in its pocket, stumping up an eye-catching $30M to cornerstone the deal, no doubt helping grease the wheels. Remarkably, the 26.5-cent placement carried zero discount to the previous closing price and was struck six per cent above the 10-day volume-weighted average. You read it right, six per cent above! The proceeds are set to advance Gorilla’s Cosmos, North Kalgoorlie and Vivien gold assets.

Advertisement

The shares touched 40.5 cents last Wednesday, a magnificent 52.8 per cent premium to issue, before easing to 36.5 cents midway through Friday, still leaving punters a handsome 38 per cent ahead. No discount, a substantial institutional book and a post-listing rocket. Somebody clearly remembered to feed the gorilla. Nice work all round! Gorilla’s performance also highlighted the different fortunes awaiting subscribers across Canaccord’s broader collection of mandates. The broker joined Commonwealth Securities, Morgans Financial, Ord Minnett and Taylor Collison on Solaris Australian Equity Income Fund’s package worth up to $91.97M.

Advertisement

That comprised a $28.5M placement and a proposed $63.47M entitlement offer at $2.02; a 5.2 per cent discount to the previous close, although a slight premium to pre-tax net tangible asset backing. At $2.06, placement subscribers were a miserly two per cent ahead, while the entitlement component remains open. It was a considerably more restrained celebration than Gorilla’s party, but still better than the reception awaiting investors in Many Peaks Minerals. Canaccord took the combined global coordinator and sole bookrunner seat on Many Peaks’ $70M placement, sharing joint lead-manager duties with Barrenjoey and SCP Resource Finance. The $1 shares were issued at a 12.3 per cent discount to fund development of the Ferke gold project in Côte d’Ivoire.

Advertisement

Yet despite that sizeable concession, the shares are currently trading at 88 cents, leaving subscribers on the wrong side of the ledger with a 12% loss. Apparently, a double-digit discount is no substitute for an uncooperative share market. The mixed results continued beyond Canaccord’s books. Petra Capital secured lead-manager and sole bookrunner duties on Pacific Lime and Cement’s $50 million placement at 36 cents, with Barrenjoey co-leading and Tamesis Partners co-managing. The proceeds are earmarked for early development work at the company’s cement project near Port Moresby in Papua New Guinea, while Tamesis also advised on a separate prospective financing arrangement.

Advertisement

Subscribers are subsequently 11.1 per cent behind at 32 cents, proving that even a business built around cement could not guarantee a solid aftermarket. Auric Mining’s Burbanks processing facility, subject to a refurbishment study, just 15km from its Union Jack project near Coolgardie. Auric Mining offered a less painful outcome. Canaccord, Taylor Collison and MA Moelis Australia Advisory shared joint lead-manager duties on its $17M placement, with Lazarus Advisory co-managing. The company also proposed a $3M share purchase plan.

Advertisement

The 18.5-cent raise will support work at Auric’s Munda, Union Jack and Iron Maiden projects, alongside potential acquisitions and an upgrade to its Burbanks processing plant. With the shares trading at 17 cents, subscribers’ noses were 8.1 per cent below the waterline. No champagne corks flying, but no need to call the family doctor either. One transaction offering a different flavour involved Western Gold Resources, where the attraction extended beyond the usual institutional placement. Taurus Capital Group took the sole lead-manager role on the $7.5M raising at eight cents, with a disclosed six per cent fee potentially delivering a sweet $450,000 clip on the full amount.

Advertisement

The placement was struck at a 2.6 per cent premium to the previous close and a 6.67 per cent premium to the 15-day VWAP. More interestingly, the highly acquisitive and soon-to-be producing gold miner Forrestania Resources committed $5.5M as a cornerstone investor, strengthening ties around Western Gold’s Gold Duke project and a recent associated ore purchase arrangement. The money is slated to support site establishment, drilling and working capital. Western Gold subsequently finished at 7.4 cents, leaving subscribers 7.5 per cent in the red. Still, Forrestania’s investment was clearly about more than chasing an immediate trading profit. Its strategic relationship gave the deal a dimension missing from many conventional placements.

Advertisement

And then came GBA Capital, which demonstrated that the smaller end of the market could produce some of the more eye-watering broker economics. GBA’s first assignment involved Sarytogan Graphite’s one-for-four entitlement offer seeking up to $3.846M at 5.8 cents - a miserly two per cent below the last closing price - plus a one-for-two, three-year oppy exercisable at 8.7 cents. The broker acted as lead manager and partially underwrote $1M, with remuneration including a $50,000 lead-manager fee, a 1.5 per cent management fee, five per cent underwriting and eligible shortfall-placement fees, plus five options for every dollar of qualifying shortfall placed, on the same terms. The Crucible’s calculator doesn’t have enough memory to do the maths on that one. Our best guess is it’s a pretty penny for underwriting a lazy million, with punters currently seven per cent down on the deal. The funds are destined to support graphite test work and feasibility activities in Kazakhstan, alongside environmental work and copper exploration.

Advertisement

However, an intriguing contrast emerged from GBA’s next two assignments. Northstone Resources raised $2.37M at 0.9 cents to advance its Tlamino gold-silver and Timok East copper projects in Serbia. GBA’s six per cent cash commission amounted to roughly $142,000, with another 26.34M broker options proposed, exercisable at two cents until January 2030, subject to shareholder approval. A tidy incentive for the broker to man the phones. For the hard-bitten thrill-seekers who subscribed, the shares have since tanked 22.2 per cent below the issue price, leaving a trail of blood from injured punters all the way to the emergency department’s door.

Advertisement

GBA then completed its hat-trick with Kuniko Limited’s $600,000 placement at 1.5 cents, collecting another six per cent cash commission worth $36,000. The board also kicked in $80k, usually a good sign. The proposed remuneration included 6.87M listed broker options exercisable at a well out-of-the-money strike price of 7 cents with a May 2029 expiry. Kuniko will use the money for further drilling at its Commonwealth-Silica Hill gold-silver project in NSW. Unfortunately, punters required a stretcher and heavy bandaging, with the shares currently trading at an unsettling 26.7 per cent below issue. Across Northstone and Kuniko alone, GBA’s disclosed cash commissions totalled$178,200, accompanied by 33.2M proposed broker options, subject to shareholder approval. Good luck with that, lads.

Those options may ultimately prove valuable or worthless. Either way, the contrast with the immediate fortunes of their placement subscribers was difficult to ignore. The broker had negotiated its cash remuneration and potential future upside. Some of the punters, meanwhile, had unknowingly been dealt a free option on a visit to ICU. The IPO market supplied one final helping of broker economics, though, when AI-focused Capability X made its ASX debut on November 12 after raising $12M at 20 cents. The company will deploy the proceeds to expand sales, fund research and development, hire technical talent and commercialise its artificial intelligence-driven industrial safety technology. Westar Capital acted as lead manager, with a six per cent fee worth $720,000 and a juicy $10,000 monthly corporate-advisory retainer extending over two years.

The handsome package also included 12M lead-manager options exercisable at 30 cents over three years. But punters won’t begrudge Westar its share of the spoils after Capability X rocketed to 31 cents on debut, a whopping 55 per cent above its 20-cent issue price, before easing to 27.5 cents. With a 37.5 per cent paper profit already in the bag, punters were grinning from ear to ear. Great work, captain. The drinks are on you! Meanwhile, in the good old USA... Wall Street’s AI feeding frenzy reached fever pitch overnight as Claude creator Anthropic stormed onto the Nasdaq in an eye-watering US$81.3 billion (A$122B) IPO. Priced at US$83 (A$124.70), the shares rocketed nearly 39 per cent on debut to US$115.10 (A$173). The stock eventually settled at US$97.17 (A$146), still a handsome 17 per cent premium and valuing the AI heavyweight at roughly US$1.76 trillion (A$2.64T). Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley led a veritable army of investment bankers into the deal, with the underwriting syndicate pocketing a coffee-spitting US$550M (A$826M) in fees. Not a bad night’s work for the corporate suits. Who said the AI market was in trouble? And so, another fortnight drew to a close with brokers pocketing their commissions, underwriting fees and potential option windfalls, while subscribers experienced everything from Gorilla’s 52.8 per cent gain and Capability X’s 55 per cent triumph to Kuniko’s 26.7 per cent tumble and Paladin’s 22.3 per cent loss.

title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
